#10473. Google’s Intelligent Eyewear glasses from Gentle Monster are already sold out

One of the first partner brands selling Android XR glasses, “Intelligent Eyewear” as Google calls it, has already completely sold out, with Gentle Monster no longer accepting pre-orders just days after launch.

Google’s Gemini-powered Intelligent Eyewear lineup launched last week with collections from Gentle Monster and Warby Parker, with pricing starting at $395. Just a few days later, though, over half of the lineup is sold out.

Every single Intelligent Eyewear style from Gentle Monster is currently sold out, with pre-orders no longer available.

Warby Parker, meanwhile, still has most styles fully in stock. Some are delayed, mainly “Reid” which has the wide fit delayed as far as December 28, but others are still shipping on launch day.

It’s unclear how many units were actually available, so it’s tough to say whether or not these are actually a hit yet, but it’s certainly unexpected to see a whole collection sold out this quickly. The first batch of Android XR glasses go on sale on December 10 – are you getting a pair?

#10472. Why Big Tech and memory chip stocks are getting a boost today

It’s a good day to be an investor in a tech stock, with shares of companies from Alphabet to Micron up in premarket trading.

Concerns over an AI bubble, the Nvidia scandal, and global instability have led to some slumps recently. The tech-heavy Nasdaq is down 7.57% over the last month as of Wednesday’s close.

Now it looks like a turnaround could be within reach as Anthropic, maker of the Claude AI chatbot, is set to make its IPO. 

No matter how far under a rock you are, it’s hard to avoid the news of Anthropic’s market debut and the impact it could have on both the tech industry and stock market.

Anthropic is the first fully AI company of this size to go public, and its high valuation sends a clear signal to investors that the demand for AI is there. As reported by the Financial Times, the company raised a record-breaking $107 billion in the offering (including a private placement). 

So, how are the biggest tech stocks shaking out ahead of Anthropic’s IPO? Let’s start with the Magnificent 7:

  • Alphabet Inc. (Nasdaq: GOOG): up 4.15%
  • Amazon.com, Inc. (Nasdaq: AMZN): up 2.14%
  • Apple Inc. (Nasdaq: AAPL): up 0.41%
  • Meta Platforms, Inc. (Nasdaq: META): up 1.47%
  • Microsoft Corporation (Nasdaq: MSFT): up 1.22%
  • Nvidia Corporation (Nasdaq: NVDA): up 1.58%
  • Tesla, Inc. (Nasdaq: TSLA): up 1.93%

Then there’s memory chip companies, which are seeing a significant boost across the board: 

  • Micron Technology, Inc. (Nasdaq: MU): up 4.97%
  • SanDisk Corporation (Nasdaq: SNDK): up 4.74%
  • Seagate Technology Holdings plc (Nasdaq: STX): up 5.75%
  • Western Digital Corporation (Nasdaq: WDC): up 5.56%

Over on South Korea’s Kospi Index, SK Hynix and Samsung closed up 3.41% and 1.13%, respectively, on Thursday. 

What’s the latest with Anthropic’s IPO?

On Thursday, Anthropic will make its stock market debut on Nasdaq with the ticker ANT. The company is listing its shares at $83, an increase from its earlier estimate of $70 to $78 per share, making for a valuation of up to $1.5 trillion. The offering will include 980 million shares of Class A common stock.

#10471. Anthropic stock closes 17% higher on its first trading day as Nasdaq sputters

Update Thursday: 4:05 p.m.

Shares of Anthropic, PBC closed 17% above their offering price on Thursday in a sign that investor interest in the AI revolution has not waned, although the enthusiasm was not enough to lift other Big Tech companies in the space.

The Claude maker’s stock opened at $111.50 a share on its first trading day, well above its $83-per-share IPO price, but then it fell shortly afterward, closing the day at $97.17.

Much of the Nasdaq did not fare so well, with AI-adjacent companies including Alphabet, Meta Platforms, Amazon, and SpaceX all down between 2%-4%, despite seeing an early-morning lift during premarket trading as interest in Anthropic’s listing hit fever pitch.

Anthropic raised a record-breaking $81.3 billion in its IPO. Now all eyes will be on how it and its peers perform in the days and weeks ahead. Shares were down slighly in after-hours trading shortly after the closing bell.

Update Thursday, 12:35 p.m.

Shares of Anthropic, PBC opened at $111.50 on Thursday in the year’s most hyped stock market debut. That’s roughly 34% higher than the $83 share price set before trading began—itself an increase over the AI giant’s original target range.

However, the stock quickly began to fall in the first hour and was trading at around $99 a share as of this writing.

Much of the market also moved lower, with the Nasdaq down around 0.73% as of 12:40 p.m. ET.

Original story:

Today, the most hyped IPO of the year (and that’s saying something) is expected to finally take place.

Claude LLM maker Anthropic, PBC (Nasdaq: ANT) will debut on the Nasdaq to much fanfare and lofty expectations. But while the Nasdaq opens at 9:30 a.m. ET, it’s likely Anthropic’s shares will not begin trading to the general public until later.

Here’s what you need to know.

The largest IPO in history

Today is Anthropic’s market debut, and its shares will begin trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT. The initial public offering is the largest in history, surpassing SpaceX’s $75 billion IPO in June. The AI giant raised $81.3 billion in the offering.

The forthcoming stock listing is also the most-hyped of the year.

As Fast Company previously noted, Anthropic is considered a pure-play AI company. That is, the company’s sole business is artificial intelligence, as opposed to, say, SpaceX, which is mainly a space transportation and telecommunications company first, and an AI company second.

As the largest pure-play AI IPO ever, there’s a lot riding on how the shares react. If investors scoop them up and the share price pops, it could suggest that Wall Street still has an appetite for riskier AI-related stocks, despite recent pullbacks in the broader tech market.

However, don’t expect to know how ANT shares are performing as soon as the Nasdaq opens at 9:30 a.m. ET. That’s because, despite the market open, the first buy and sell orders for ANT shares likely won’t be fulfilled until later in the day.

What time do Anthropic’s shares begin trading today?

If a stock is already listed on an exchange, its shares usually begin trading to the public as soon as that exchange opens. But for market debuts, things are a little different.

Stock exchanges know that there is frequently a flurry of orders (both buy and sell) when a hot stock debuts.

If the stock were to trade immediately when the market opened, it could cause extreme price volatility, sending the stock up or down significantly in a matter of seconds. Another reason is operational: Nasdaq simply needs time to match orders—buyers with sellers—and determine a price.

Because of this, markets like the Nasdaq have procedures in place that delay trading by a little bit so buyers and sellers can get a better idea of demand and price the stock accordingly. Nasdaq calls this a Halt Cross.

Only once Nasdaq has determined an opening clearing price based on all its buy and sell orders does it release the stock for trading.

Why does this sound familiar?

If this sounds familiar, it’s because it’s exactly the same process that happened with the SpaceX IPO.

While SPCX shares debuted on the Nasdaq on June 12, they did not begin trading immediately when the Nasdaq opened at 9:30 a.m. ET. Instead, SpaceX’s shares began trading about two to three hours after the morning bell.

So, what time, then, will Anthropic’s shares actually begin trading on the Nasdaq?

It’s impossible to say for sure. Nasdaq’s rules don’t restrict the Halt Cross to a certain defined period, such as two hours. The Halt Cross lasts as long as it needs to.

However, if history is any indication, the Halt Cross usually ends anywhere from 2-4 hours after markets open.

That rough estimate suggests that Anthropic shares will begin trading at some point roughly between 11:30 a.m. ET and 1:30 p.m. ET today.

#10470. Someone rebuilt old Android versions in your browser, and it’s an instant nostalgia hit [Gallery]

The “Android Time Machine” is a fun project that puts Android versions into your browser, giving you a quick and easy chance to play around with older versions for a quick hit of nostalgia.

Built on the back of AOSP builds for classic Nexus devices, “Android Time Machine” lets you quickly access older Android versions. Specifically, Android 2.1 Eclair through Android 7.1.2 Nougat.

The simulator runs within the shell of a matching Nexus smartphone on a desktop browser, or to fit your actual smartphone if you run it on Android.

Versions and simulated smartphones include:

The best part here is how it works on your actual smartphone. When launched in fullscreen, it scales to match your phone’s screen – meaning it fits even devices like the Galaxy Z Fold 8’s smaller outer display (it just shows the desktop version when open).

Since this is running through the browser and not an actual Android build, you won’t get a perfect replication. Performance is a little hit or miss, especially with certain animations, but it works really well overall.

The browser even simulates results from each era (oh, to go back to when Google Search wasn’t an absolute mess). Similarly, Google apps and the camera are filled with placeholders since the web app can’t access the actual camera or connect to the internet to sign into a Google account.

Seeing things like the boot animations and live wallpapers from classic Nexus phones, as well as peeking back at lost apps like Google+ and Play Music, is just such a fun little piece of nostalgia.

“Android Time Machine” is free, and the source code is available on GitHub.

#10467. The real lesson businesses should learn from video games (it’s more than ‘gamification’)

In the early 2000s I (Bing) found myself crouched in an office cubicle frantically scribbling down a few things I thought the video game industry could teach a burgeoning online bookstore.

I was initially reluctant when my friend, the legendary venture capitalist John Doerr, asked me to take a meeting in Seattle with a buzzy, young startup CEO. I was a midcareer video game executive and this particular founder had already been named Time’s 1999 person of the year. Terrified to look a fool, I ducked into a cubicle at the Electronic Arts office in Seattle and outlined an idea for an online customer loyalty program based on the strategy that had turned Madden NFL into a forever franchise by giving gamers reasons to come back year after year.

I practically stuffed the one-pager in Jeff Bezos’s hand the first time we met over coffee. He laughed, but indulged me and unfurled the page. I started my career in video games as a marketing chief, and I was still in the habit of writing headline copy for all my one-pagers. Across the top of this one I wrote: Amazon Prime.

Jeff would say that Prime’s success was a good surprise, but when you know video games, when you understand the magical ways that they tap into our intrinsic motivations and make us want to come back again and again, you understand that game design thinking has the potential to increase retention and engagement in almost any walk of life. After Amazon Prime worked so well, I brought the lessons of video games to all kinds of consumer industries, from entertainment products like Spotify to financial products like Better Mortgage to educational products like Coursera and Duolingo and even weight loss apps like My Fitness Pal.

A bad rap

I used to call the craft of applying video game design to consumer products “video gamification,” but these days gamification has a bad rap. Some of the smartest business minds I know brush it off as a short-lived 2010s trend that didn’t pan out. I’ve heard countless product teams complain that the points and leaderboard systems they build into their user interfaces didn’t make a dent in any of their retention metrics. Worse still, I have friends and peers who recoil when they hear the word “gamify,” immediately assuming someone is trying to manipulate their time and attention. Gamification has taken on such a negative connotation that I’ve stopped using the word altogether.

The thing is, the so-called “gamification” trend that failed hard in the 2010s was based on a fundamental misunderstanding of what makes successful games work. Product teams that couldn’t figure out how to boost traffic to their app would probably be surprised to learn that successful games rarely rely on competition to motivate players. In fact, in video games, cooperation is a far more important mechanism than competition.

Connection, mastery, productivity

If you’re going to channel the motivational magic of a great game, you need to understand what actually goes into crafting one. The top reasons that players come back to a game are, in order of importance, social connection, personal mastery, and productivity. Most business execs I meet assume that productivity measures like money and rankings are the most important motivational forces, but the video game industry has found for decades that social relationships and the satisfaction of self-improvement far outweigh them.

In the early days of the Facebook juggernaut game Farmville, its developer, Zynga, found that the notifications that invited friends to play cooperatively garnered 30 times the clicks that the competitive, brag-based notifications did. In games, a two-way social interaction is the top predictor of whether or not somebody comes back tomorrow.

Nongamers find this surprising, but they shouldn’t! We’re human beings, ever motivated to build communities and deepen our relationships with one another. We come back to the games and products that best align with that. One of the great social features of the business networking platform Linkedin is “Endorsements,” where users are invited to publicly vouch for their peers and strengthen their professional relationships. Cooperative features like this give people a reason to return to the résumé sharing platform regularly, even when they aren’t searching for jobs.

Personal mastery and self-improvement are also intrinsic motivators to every gamer. Mechanics that give people a framework to measure and track self-improvement, like experience points and level-ups, create an invigorating sense of progress with each session. Scores are important in games, but more so as a way to rate individual progression instead of rank it against others.

Productivity measures like time saved and money earned also motivate us, especially when they’re paired with our social and mastery priorities. We like earning money, sure, but we love earning money doing things we already wanted to do, and we might forgo it when it comes in direct conflict with our social relationships and sense of self-worth.

More of what they want

Amazon Prime works because it gives its customers more of what they already want. Free and fast shipping offers an incredible productivity proposition, especially in terms of time saved, and individualized customer profiles help us form identities around ourselves as consumers. Amazon knows that one of the biggest predictors of whether a Prime user renews is how often they use their subscription benefits, but pushing members to make purchases they otherwise wouldn’t risks undermining long-term loyalty. So Amazon treats Prime like a forever game franchise, continually improving the experience and layering on new benefits like Prime Video, Amazon Music, and prescription savings. Each gives members another reason to use their subscription in ways that already align with their interests.

When I gut check a user experience to see if it’s aligned with my own wants and needs, it’s usually as simple as asking, does this product like me? Do I feel better about myself at the end of my session than I did at the beginning? If the answer is no, it usually means the designers are trying to gamify me against my own best interest, like a credit card rewards program that persuades me to spend more money than I would otherwise, or a social media platform that delivers empty dopamine hits without any meaningful upside to my social relationships.

These days, I’ve dropped the term “gamification,” but my belief in applying game thinking to products hasn’t wavered. Start with what people actually want, and build around those priorities. You’ll tap into intrinsic motivations far more powerful than any user interface trick or attention hack. That’s real video gamification, and that will always work.

#10466. No ‘credible pathway’ for the energy sector to return to the pre-Iran war days, says IEA

The world’s largest energy shock in history and growing climate change concerns this year are reshaping the future of how people will power homes, drive cars and fuel industries, according to an International Energy Agency report released Thursday.

The energy crisis, triggered by the Iran war, will “leave lasting marks” on the world’s energy sector, according to the Paris-based IEA, founded after the 1973-74 energy crisis.

Energy-hungry nations will prioritize the security and affordability of their electricity, the report said. This is a boon for renewable technologies, like solar, and alternative technologies, like nuclear. But it is also reinforcing the case to keep coal as a backup in times of crisis.

This is especially true in coal-rich Asia, which went into energy triage when the Iran war cut off the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow passageway where around a fifth of the world’s traded oil typically flows.

The report looks “past the current turmoil to explore the range of energy futures that could emerge from today’s upheaval,” said IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol. He said the Iran war “delivered a huge shock to the system” and warned “the longer the crisis lasts, the deeper the effects will be.”

“I don’t see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before,” he said.

Annual United Nations climate talks, known as COP31 and hosted in Turkey this year, are in their second and final week. Before these negotiations, the U.N. announced the world is dangerously close to missing its goal of limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial temperatures.

Electrification — the process of powering homes, cars and industries with electricity — and moving away from planet-warming fossil fuels are the two big ticket issues at this year’s climate talks.

“The future of the energy system and our climate are inextricably intertwined,” said Rachel Cleetus, climate program director at the Union of Concerned Scientists, who is at COP31.

Flagship report forecasts energy future

The IEA, the world’s leading intergovernmental energy organization with more than 30 member countries, publishes World Energy Outlooks annually.

This year’s 560-page plus report analyzes government and private data to project various future scenarios based on whether countries will continue with current policies or drastically change policies in the face of ongoing crises.

The world’s energy sector will clearly have a before and after the Iran war, experts said. In March, the IEA coordinated the emergency release of 400 million barrels of crude oil stocks to stabilize global markets.

“This crisis has exposed the price of fossil fuel dependence,” said Mohamed Adow, director of Power Shift Africa. “It’s crazy that a conflict thousands of miles away can send energy bills soaring at home.”

Conflicts, trade tensions, climate risks and cyberattacks are increasing the number of possible energy futures. The IEA said the “drive to diversify” fuel supplies will reshape the energy trade.

The Middle East will still be the world’s largest oil exporter, but nations will likely reduce dependence on the Strait of Hormuz. The IEA forecasts the amount of oil transiting the strait could go from 20 million barrels per day before the Iran war, to 8.5 million barrels in 2030, and even under 2 million barrels by 2035.

While fossil fuels still dominate national energy mixes, the IEA said renewables — led by solar — and nuclear power are the “biggest beneficiaries” of governments trying to grow domestic energy sources. But energy security concerns may lead coal-rich nations to rely on the fossil fuel as a fallback option during times of crisis.

“When we look at how energy crises change the world over the long term, governments are only just beginning to get their head around just how much things will change,” said Dave Jones, co-founder of the think tank Ember.

Climate talks eye electrification

The ongoing talks in Turkey follow a year rattled by the Iran war’s energy shock, as well as several climate-induced disasters.

Global warming adds pressure to rising electricity demand. In what the IEA called a “striking milestone,” energy demand for cooling is overtaking energy demand for heating for the first time.

India, the world’s most populous nation, will account for more energy demand growth over the next decade than any other country or region. China, already one of the world’s most electrified economies, may see its electrification grow from 32% last year to 43% by 2035 — the highest among any major economy.

At COP31, Turkey is pushing for the world to increase the share of electricity in total global energy consumption from roughly 21% today to 35% by 2035.

While the preference would be for this to come from renewable energy, U.N. documents on the negotiating table don’t spell this out. That means coal and other fossil fuels could be used, at least initially.

“The IEA’s latest report makes clear that the fossil energy crisis unleashed by the US-Israel war on Iran has irrevocably changed the global energy system, adding to the many reasons why countries would benefit from a rapid transition to clean energy and electrification,” said Cleetus, with the Union of Concerned Scientists.

The Associated Press’ climate and environmental coverage receives financial support from multiple private foundations. The AP is solely responsible for all content. Find AP’s standards for working with philanthropies, a list of supporters and funded coverage areas at AP.org.

—Anton L. Delgado and Sibi Arasu, Associated Press

#10464. Pixel Journal update rolls out Recorder integration, file export [U]

Following the last update in August, Google is rolling out a sizable update to Pixel Journal that adds Recorder audio entries and file exports.

Update 11/16: Updates for Pixel Journal (version 2026.10.27.x) and Pixel Recorder (4.2.20261001.x) are widely rolling out. After installing (be sure to open the apps and Force stop), you’ll see “Record new audio” and “Add existing recording” in the Add item menu.

The first option directly launches the Recorder app into a new session, while the second brings up a list of previous recordings. The Journal app will show an inline audio player and transcript, which can be removed.

Curiously, these updates weren’t mentioned as part of the November 2026 Pixel Drop.

Journal November 2026 updates:• Recorder integration: Record new audio or add existing recordings from Pixel Recorder, complete with playable clips and transcripts• Journal export: Export your entries and media to view offline anytime

Original 11/10: From the “Add item” plus menu in entries, you’ll see “Record new audio” join the existing Take photo/video, Add photo, Health Connect activity, and location & map options.

At the moment, this audio integration is not live as Pixel Recorder also requires an update that we’re not seeing in the Play Store yet.

Being able to add a “voice entry with audio” is a pretty common feature for journaling apps. A transcription capability looks to be available for Google’s implementation.

Meanwhile, in Pixel Journal settings, there’s a new “Export your journal” option. This creates a ZIP file of all your entries, including images. Text is exported as HTML files.

Version 2026.10.27.x of Pixel Journal is still rolling out via Google Play today.

#10463. Preventing API Contract Drift in TypeScript Applications

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A frontend application can compile successfully and still fail when it communicates with the backend.

Imagine a backend developer changes an API response from:

The backend works correctly. The frontend also builds without errors. However, a component expecting user.name now receives undefined.

This is an example of API contract drift: the frontend and backend no longer agree on the structure or behavior of an API.

The problem becomes more difficult when several developers or teams work on different parts of an application. A change made by one team may affect another team's assumptions without producing an obvious error during development.

TypeScript helps catch many programming mistakes, but its types do not automatically validate data received over HTTP. A type declaration can describe what the application expects without proving that the server actually returns it.

In this tutorial, we'll look at a practical way to make API contracts more reliable.

Consider a typical frontend API function:

The function promises to return a User, so TypeScript allows the application to access properties such as name and email.

The return value of response.json() is not automatically checked against the User interface. The interface only provides compile-time information; it does not validate the actual JSON received from the server.

the frontend may still treat the response as a User even though the data has a different structure.

This is particularly important when working with:

Independently deployed frontend and backend applications.

APIs maintained by different engineering teams.

The solution is to validate data at the boundary where it enters the application.

Zod is a TypeScript-first schema validation library. It allows developers to describe expected data structures and validate actual values against those definitions.

Now create a schema for the user response:

First, UserSchema describes the structure that the application expects at runtime.

Second, z.infer generates the corresponding TypeScript type from the schema.

This means developers do not need to maintain a separate interface and validation definition for the same data structure.

The response is initially treated as unknown, which prevents the application from assuming that untrusted data already has the expected structure.

UserSchema.parse() validates the actual response.

If the backend returns an unexpected property type or misses a required field, Zod throws a validation error instead of allowing invalid data to move silently through the application.

You can also use safeParse() when you prefer to handle validation errors without exceptions:

This approach is useful when API responses are external or when a frontend must provide more controlled error handling.

One common mistake is placing API validation logic directly inside React components.

For a small application, this may seem convenient. As the project grows, however, it becomes difficult to reuse validation rules and identify where data transformations happen.

A better approach is to separate API schemas, service functions, and UI components.

The responsibilities are straightforward:

schemas/user.ts defines the expected user data.

api/client.ts handles common HTTP configuration.

api/users.ts contains user-related API requests.

hooks/useUser.ts manages data fetching for React.

components/UserProfile.tsx displays the validated data.

This structure makes it easier to change an API implementation without rewriting the UI.

It also makes testing more manageable because validation logic can be tested independently of React rendering.

For more ideas on organizing application code, see SitePoint's guide to modern JavaScript modules.

Runtime validation protects an application when data arrives. However, teams also need a shared description of what an API is supposed to accept and return.

OpenAPI provides a standard format for describing HTTP APIs, including:

For example, an endpoint can be described using an OpenAPI document:

This document describes what the endpoint should return.

Both frontend and backend developers can refer to the same contract instead of relying on separate assumptions or outdated documentation.

Swagger Editor helps developers write and validate OpenAPI documents. It also provides a convenient way to inspect API definitions.

Swagger UI turns an OpenAPI document into interactive API documentation, allowing developers to explore endpoints and test requests.

Redoc provides another way to generate readable API documentation from an OpenAPI specification.

These tools are particularly useful when APIs are maintained by multiple developers or consumed by several applications.

Maintaining API types manually across frontend and backend repositories creates opportunities for inconsistencies.

For example, a backend developer might add a new optional property while the frontend continues using an older interface.

One way to reduce this duplication is to generate TypeScript definitions and API clients from an OpenAPI specification.

Orval is a useful tool for this workflow.

It can generate TypeScript clients and types from an OpenAPI document, helping frontend developers work with consistent endpoint definitions.

A typical configuration might look like this:

The exact configuration depends on the Orval version and the structure of the OpenAPI document.

Once configured, the client can be regenerated when the API specification changes.

This reduces the amount of repetitive code developers need to maintain manually.

However, generated types should not be confused with runtime validation. They improve consistency during development, but an application may still need to validate responses received from external systems or services that cannot be fully trusted.

Frontend developers often need to build or test features before the corresponding backend endpoint is ready.

Waiting for a complete backend implementation can slow down development, particularly when multiple teams work independently.

Mock Service Worker (MSW) helps solve this problem by intercepting network requests and returning controlled responses.

You can define a mock handler for the user endpoint:

The frontend can now make normal HTTP requests while MSW supplies predictable responses during development or testing.

You can also simulate an invalid response:

This makes it possible to check whether the application's validation and error-handling logic behave as expected.

MSW is particularly valuable because it allows frontend tests to run without requiring a live backend environment.

Runtime validation and generated clients improve reliability, but they do not automatically guarantee that independently developed services remain compatible.

For systems with multiple services, contract testing can provide another layer of protection.

Pact is a contract-testing tool that allows consumers and providers to verify their expectations about API interactions.

Consider a frontend application that expects the user endpoint to return:

The consumer defines the expected interaction.

The backend provider can then run verification against that contract to check whether its actual response satisfies the consumer's expectations.

This helps identify breaking changes before they reach production.

These tools solve different problems. A project does not necessarily need all of them, but larger applications can benefit from combining the approaches that match their architecture.

A contract is only useful if developers consistently check it when making changes.

A practical approach is to run validation and tests automatically whenever someone opens a pull request.

For example, a GitHub Actions workflow might look like this:

The api:validate script should be configured to validate the project's OpenAPI document or run the relevant contract checks.

The test command should execute the application's automated tests.

For a production project, you may also want to include:

The objective is to detect incompatible changes before they are merged.

A failed pipeline gives developers an opportunity to investigate the change while the context is still fresh.

API contracts become harder to maintain when several teams contribute to the same system.

For example, a company might have separate teams responsible for:

If nobody owns an API contract, small changes can create unexpected problems for other teams.

Assigning clear ownership helps establish who reviews changes, maintains documentation, and coordinates breaking updates.

This becomes particularly important when an organization expands its engineering capacity across locations or adds several specialized teams. Companies planning that kind of growth may also need to consider enterprise IT recruitment as part of their wider engineering workforce strategy.

Regardless of how a team is assembled, its development process should establish clear responsibilities for API design, versioning, testing, and release coordination.

A few practical conventions can make a significant difference:

Assign an owner to every important API or service.

Document breaking changes before implementation.

Require contract-related tests in pull requests.

Keep generated clients synchronized with the API specification.

Communicate deprecations before removing existing fields.

Monitor production errors after deploying API changes.

These practices help prevent a growing engineering organization from becoming a collection of disconnected services.

API contract drift is not simply a TypeScript problem. It is a coordination problem that becomes visible when applications and services develop different expectations about the same data.

TypeScript provides useful compile-time checks, but it cannot guarantee that an HTTP response matches a declared interface.

A more reliable approach combines several techniques:

Use OpenAPI to document API expectations.

Generate TypeScript clients with tools such as Orval.

Use MSW to test frontend behavior without a live backend.

Use Pact when consumer-provider contract verification is appropriate.

Run validation and tests automatically in CI/CD.

You do not need to introduce every tool at once. Start by validating external API responses, document important endpoints, and gradually automate contract checks as the application grows.

The result is a codebase where developers can make changes with greater confidence and where frontend and backend teams have a shared understanding of how their systems communicate.

#10462. Instagram now lets you edit stories, but you have to act fast. Here’s how to do it

For anyone who has ever hit share, only to spot a typo moments later, Instagram now has a fix for that. The Meta-owned platform is rolling out a feature that lets you edit a story after you post it. 

Instagram head Adam Mosseri announced the new feature Wednesday in a post on his Instagram feed.

“A lot of people have been asking for this, so I’m excited to get this one out there,” he shared in the post.

You can edit text, music, stickers, and drawings, but there’s one catch: you have to act fast. You can only make edits to a story within 15 minutes of sharing.

You can fix typos and other mistakes without losing your views, likes, or replies. Previously, the only option besides leaving the story up was to delete it and repost.

A few other details worth knowing 

When you edit a story, Instagram adds an edited label, and your audience stays the same.

Any previous reshares of the story get removed. According to Instagram, editing is not available on stories that were also shared to Facebook or contain certain stickers.

How to edit an Instagram story:

  1. Open your published story.
  2. Tap the three dots “More” button.
  3. Select Edit story.
  4. Fix your text, or update stickers, drawing, or music.
  5. Save the changes.

Instagram announced the feature along with other stories upgrades, including new sticker designs, an easier way to select multiple photos, and backgrounds for photos of any size.

A small but welcome potential reprieve for PC builders and consumers.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Solid-state drives, phones, laptops, and tablets have all gotten substantially pricier in the last couple of years. Beyond the stratospheric prices of DDR5 memory, prospective PC builders and consumer electronics buyers have had to deal with upcharges on SSDs of all sizes thanks to the AI boom. That may be changing soon, as spot pricing for consumer NAND chips is reportedly dropping, according to a new report from Seoul Economic Daily (SED).

The report observes a 20% drop in spot pricing for NAND chips over just the last month. Its conclusions are bolstered by information from a Bank of America note from Nov. 13, wherein industry sources tell that institution that NAND is due for a market correction.

SED says that according to that note, 512 Gb NAND wafers saw a 32% drop to $14.30 apiece on the spot market, while 1 Tb wafers fell 19% to $24.90. SED quotes another industry source that says: "NAND cannot sustain the steep price gains seen so far."

Those decreases may be hard to square in a time when enterprise SSDs are getting pricier by the day, but SED notes that the rise in phone and PC prices has led customers to delay upgrades, resulting in a 20% year-on-year decline in shipments for phones alone and making for the lowest third-quarter volumes in 14 years. Meanwhile, PC shipments have also fallen 22.5% year-on-year, according to a Gartner report.

In the face of those consumer decisions, device makers are letting their existing stock drain out and are presumably stocked with NAND chips for the short term, thus resulting in lower prices for new fab shipments on the short-term spot market.

Another factor in the consumer NAND market is that not all flash is equal. Both RAM and NAND makers have been redirecting their chip output to serve the ongoing AI boom, converting their consumer-grade production lines to make higher-spec silicon. Memory factories have been converting DDR5 capacity to HBM at a steady pace, as parts of the process are shared across both types.

But according to the Bank of America note that SED cites, things are different in the NAND world. High-density flash now sits at around 300 layers, and its production requires substantially different tooling compared to the lower-grade silicon deemed suitable for us mere mortals. So the continuing growth in NAND demand from AI data centers may not translate directly into reduced consumer supply.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Beyond those factors, added supply from Chinese NAND maker YMTC is creating additional downward price pressure in the NAND market. SED notes that YMTC has taken a 14% chunk from major players in the NAND market in the second quarter of this year alone.

On net, these forces could result in a bit of relief for consumer tech. SED says Bank of America expects consumer NAND prices for PCs and smartphones to fall 5% to 10% on the longer-term contract market in the first quarter of 2027, while enterprise NAND contract prices are expected to hold more or less steady.

Whether those declines translate to lower prices for finished devices and components like SSDs will remain to be seen, and products with those chips inside will require some time to reach the market. But in the ongoing AI supply crunch, any potential relief is worth celebrating.

#10458. What does the Anthropic IPO mean for your 401(k)?

You may have no interest in investing in AI companies, and you may even suspect that the AI boom is a bubble about to pop. But you could already have a stake in one of the industry’s biggest players anyway: Anthropic, which went public today, may be in your retirement account or about to show up there.

Some mutual funds, including American Funds Growth Fund of America (AGTHX) and Fidelity Select Technology (FSPTX), hold substantial equity stakes in Anthropic. And some index funds will also soon acquire shares, after recently changing their rules to make it easier for massive companies to join shortly after going public. Previously, companies often had to wait months or a year to be included in major indexes, in part because of concerns about stock volatility.

Earlier this year, ahead of the SpaceX IPO, Nasdaq shortened its waiting period from three months to 15 trading days for qualified mega-IPOs. Nasdaq argued that companies as large as SpaceX and Anthropic shouldn’t have to wait so long.

FTSE Russell has similarly shortened its waiting period to just five trading days, though inclusion depends on how many shares are available for public trading. Morningstar already had a short five-day waiting period, but relaxed its rules about available shares. The S&P 500, meanwhile, still requires companies to wait 12 months and turn a profit before joining—two hurdles Anthropic has yet to clear.

When Anthropic is included in a retirement portfolio, it won’t have a large weight initially, Rodney Comegys, chief investment officer at Vanguard Capital Management and head of global equity at Vanguard, tells Fast Company. That’s because a relatively small portion of the company’s shares will be available to public investors to begin with. Vanguard has estimated that Anthropic will represent 0.05%–0.15% of its total market index fund. If you have $500,000 in that fund, that might mean $250 to $750 worth of indirect exposure to Anthropic.

How to find Anthropic in your 401(k)

To know if your 401(k) or an index fund you own will include Anthropic, you’ll have to dig into the details. “Most people don’t look at their index funds, or anything that their 401(k) is invested in,” says John Polonis, a former Wall Street lawyer who now writes about finance. Even if you’ve chosen not to invest in the Nasdaq-100, for example, the stock could still be hiding somewhere else. Other funds, including those that invest in the largest publicly traded companies, could also hold Anthropic shares. “There may be ways that you are getting exposure,” Polonis says, “and if you don’t want any exposure at all, you really have to do a lot of diligence to kind of screen that.”

To check your own portfolio, log into your 401(k) account. If you have actively managed mutual funds, look up each fund’s portfolio holdings and search for Anthropic. If you have index funds, check to see which indexes they track. The indexes that will soon acquire Anthropic stock include Russell 1000, Russell 3000, Nasdaq-100, Morningstar U.S., FTSE Global All Cap, and MSCI USA.

Because companies like Alphabet and Amazon also own large chunks of Anthropic stock, index funds also have exposure through those companies.

The risk for passive investors is low at this point because exposure is limited. But exposure is likely to grow over time. And some critics argue that because Anthropic is still at an early stage, and not yet profitable, it shouldn’t be part of retirement accounts. Jonathan Westin, executive director of Climate Organizing Hub and part of a group called Stop Funding Billionaires that protested in front of Anthropic’s offices in advance of the IPO, argues that the company’s early investors stand to reap enormous profits while ordinary investors shoulder the risk if the AI boom collapses. “They’re all just trying to get paid out and get paid out now before the collapse,” he says. “And then the real people that are left picking up the pieces are our 401(k)s and pension funds that are going to drop.”

There’s a broader issue: major indexes are supposed to reflect the market, not shape it. But fast-tracking stocks like Anthropic arguably influences the market, says Michael Green, an investor and financial market researcher who is CEO of Tier1 Alpha Asset Management. When a new company is added to a major index and index funds automatically have to buy it, that drives up the company’s stock price. A recent study calculated that fast-tracked IPOs have a 5% price premium over those added to indexes more slowly. Index funds are stuck paying prices that are inflated by their own demand. Fast-tracked companies can also raise 6.2% more capital.

“The far more important question is whether or not is it appropriate to use a platform like an index fund to facilitate a particular class of IPO that largely serves to enrich a subset of the population on the back of a government-mandated retirement system,” Green says.

And therein lies the broader problem: Green argues that the system could give the biggest companies a disproportionate advantage over smaller competitors, reinforcing an economy increasingly dominated by big business.

#10454. As widespread tech outages pile up, AI tools are in the spotlight again

Inaccessible email inboxes. Banking delays. And a communications meltdown that grounded airplanes for hours, followed by waves of other travel disruptions.

In an increasingly interconnected world, some fear such disruptions could be the new normal.

Over the past week alone, problems that appeared to emerge from routine updates, security patches or other malfunctions surfaced at Microsoft, JP Morgan Chase and Apple, and even the U.S. government’s Federal Aviation Administration and National Security Agency. The Trump administration said there was “zero” indication the latest outages are linked, or caused by bad actors like cybercriminals.

The era of artificial intelligence has also raised the stakes for internet security overall. As AI tools uncover new vulnerabilities, many other companies and institutions are racing to patch them before they can be targeted by hackers, a cat-and-mouse game that can lead to a different set of glitches.

Social media platforms have been abuzz with a mixture of annoyance, confusion, conspiracy theories and jokes about the string of outages.

“To see several disruptions this close together, I think to a lot of people it’s made them realize how many parts of their lives they’ve handed over to these systems that we still, at this point, don’t fully understand,” Jake Smith, a content creator who regularly posts videos about politics on platforms like Instagram and YouTube, said in an interview. “I think it gives people a sense of helplessness to see all of it happening concurrently in a way.”

What’s gone offline recently

Outages and technology errors have piled up across sectors.

Late last week, a global Microsoft outage disrupted email and other workplace tools, plunging business and everyday services into disarray worldwide. Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot, were interrupted. Microsoft cited, in part, a failure during a recent upgrade to its servers, spanning from what the company later determined was a “latent defect” in a network fix it had begun deploying over the summer.

For air travel, a separate malfunction in the FAA’s network led to the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years on Friday. The stop lasted for more than four hours, and carriers cancelled and delayed swaths of flights as they worked to recover. Just days later, United Airlines saw its own system outage — forcing it to delay departing flights on Monday.

Online banking troubles also piled up on Monday. JPMorgan Chase said a software bug affected its internal hardware systems — causing transactional delays for its customers and others sending money to related accounts, sending jitters throughout the financial system before the problem was resolved.

And on Tuesday, Apple, Marriott and the NSA joined the growing list. Apple Music, the App Store and AppleCare services were temporarily disrupted after the company said an internal update caused outages. And Marriott said a technical issue also caused problems for sign-ins on its website and app.

Meanwhile, the NSA said an internal network it uses to communicate classified information was also offline Tuesday “during scheduled routine maintenance.”

The government — as well as Microsoft, United, JPMorgan Chase, Apple and Marriott — have again maintained there’s no evidence of these disruptions being linked or related to a cyberattack.

Microsoft also noted that its outage did not span from “AI / agents,” although it didn’t immediately specify the goal of the network fix it first deployed over the summer. Microsoft did not respond to an Associated Press request for further details, and the other companies did not provide additional comments Wednesday about their disruptions when contacted by the AP via email.

AI has helped identify vulnerabilities, but also adds to risks

AI has nonetheless come into the spotlight as experts evaluate these disruptions — both between heightened risks posed by the technology as well as its ability to detect security gaps.

For example, AI recently helped detect sweeping vulnerabilities for PHP, a general-purpose scripting language that powers websites around the world — leading to urgent calls for updates. And that security work has resulted in some limited outages and service delays.

President Donald Trump’s director of national intelligence, Jay Clayton, pointed directly to patching those security gaps when discussing the NSA’s outage this week. Clayton told Fox News that the patching following last month’s PHP alert has caused some systems to “not come back up” as expected. “That is what has happened at the NSA today,” he said.

Meanwhile, also this week, cybersecurity startup Calif said it used AI to help uncover a software bug in Java, one of the world’s most widely used programming languages and crucial for many big companies. Oracle, which owns Java, later released a security update and U.S. cyber authorities issued an advisory on Wednesday urging organizations to install it.

At the same time, others warn that the AI boom could open the door to additional disruptions.

“As AI adoption accelerates, we are likely to witness more incidents of this nature,” Raj Rajarajan, director of the Institute for Cyber Security at City St George’s, University of London, said last week.

He noted a lot of today’s digital infrastructure wasn’t originally designed to handle the “computational demands of large-scale AI services.”

While recent outages haven’t been tied to hackers or a coordinated attack, he and others also pointed to cybersecurity risks more broadly.

“AI is absolutely making it way easier for attackers to go and launch cyber attacks. It is not quite as good at creating patches for bugs, like fixing problems, as it is exploiting them,” said Justin Cappos, a cybersecurity professor at New York University’s Tandon School of Engineering.

In a cybersecurity report this week, Google said hackers and cyber criminals are “moving beyond basic prompting” and using increasingly sophisticated AI techniques to devise and carry out their attacks. The report, which focused on nefarious activity rather than outages, said techniques include using large language models and “agentic frameworks” to reverse engineering security patches to uncover vulnerabilities and exploit them.

Unraveling one (of just a few) major players in our online lives

Regardless, the latest outages offer yet more examples of the cascading effects that can erupt when a central player in tech, banking, travel or even the government runs into system errors that upend services.

Democratic Sen. Mark Warner, co-chair of the U.S. Senate’s Cybersecurity Caucus, acknowledged the widespread concern — and again stressed what this means in the AI era.

“These disruptions should serve as a wake-up call. It feels like every day brings another reminder that AI is moving faster than our ability to manage its consequences,” Warner said Tuesday. He also argued that the Trump administration hadn’t shown enough interest in confronting these challenges.

Still, “based on what we know today, there is good reason to believe these disruptions are the unintended consequences of efforts to make our systems safer,” Warner added.

—Wyatte Grantham-Philips, Kelvin Chan and Kaitlyn Huamani, AP Business Writers

#10453. Samsung’s ‘Galaxy Studio’ headphones leak with touch controls, two colors

We’re only a couple of months away from our next Galaxy Unpacked, and while the expanded Galaxy S27 series is practically guaranteed to show up, the real fun tends to lie in whatever other gadgets show up alongside Samsung’s next flagship smartphone release. Based on some new leaks, it’s sure looking like the next mobile accessory on the company’s docket is a return to over-ear wireless headphones, and so far, they’re sounding pretty promising.

Samsung hasn’t produced over-ear headphones in about a decade — under its own name, at least — but it looks like that’s about to change. We hadn’t heard much in the way of details on the company’s next audio release, rumored to be named ‘Galaxy Studio,’ but a fresh leak courtesy of SamMobile is finally changing that. We’ll have to keep waiting for full renders, but these leaked graphics are giving us a general idea of what they might look like, plus a couple of key features.

Unsurprisingly, Galaxy Studio will include ANC, complete with a dedicated button to toggle the setting between its usual modes. Volume controls also could come in the shape of physical buttons, but playback controls appear to be relegated to a touch-sensitive area on its earpads, something that’s become relatively standard among the flagship headphone competition. SamMobile also reports it’ll come in “at least” black and red colorways, while a leak from earlier this month suggested rotational earcups.

Again, I don’t want to read too much into these leaked graphics, as it’s always possible the final release has a handful of changes. Based on these images, though, I’m pleasantly surprised to see Samsung avoiding an attempt at copying Apple’s AirPods Max design. The larger cups, combined with their ability to twist and turn for easy storage, sounds much closer to most (but not all) of Sony’s over-ear efforts across the last decade or so, and when it comes to headphones, there are much, much worse choices you could look to for inspiration. If Samsung can hit the right price on these — or bundle them with one of their ever-more-expensive smartphones — they could be a real winner.

It has been traveling for nearly 50 years to reach this milestone and continues into the unknown.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

NASA has confirmed that Voyager 1 is the first human-made object to reach one light-day's distance from Earth, passing the milestone today. A countdown at Orbital Radar confirmed that Voyager cruised past the threshold at a leisurely 37,844 mph just after 5 am ET on Wednesday, November 18. It means that Voyager is now more than 16 billion miles away, and that a signal from the spacecraft now takes fully 24 hours to travel the distance.

There are many astronomical numbers behind what is an extraordinary feat. Sci-fi shows casually mention light-years as if they are like a trip to the local convenience store. One light-day isn’t a distance to be derided, though. Over the last half century, hurtling through space at a cruising speed of 38,000 mph, the Voyager spacecraft has clocked about 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers).

These are probably bigger distances than you are used to fathoming. So NASA has kindly provided some context with the distances of various heavenly bodies in miles and light-speeds. For example, the Moon is 238,855 miles distant, or about 1.3 light seconds away from Earth. Due to Mars’ independent orbit around the Sun, it can take between three minutes and 22 minutes for light to travel between the red and the blue planet. Meanwhile, the Sun’s rays reach Earth, about 93 million miles away, in 20 light seconds. Now let us remind you that Voyager 1 is on the brink of being a whole light-day away.

On Wednesday, with this major milestone passed, Voyager 1’s journey will be far from over. NASA says that it is on course for an obscure star called Gliese 445, now in the constellation Ursa Minor. We’ll have to keep the champagne on ice for another 40,000 years to celebrate the fly-past of that star, though.

Voyager 1 carries a copy of the Golden Record. Like sending a message in a bottle, NASA scientists launched Voyager with the hope that someone, somewhere will eventually read the message. Moreover, the receiving aliens will need to source tech to play the record, which contains sounds, music, and the data needed to reconstruct photos that showcase the diversity of life and culture on our planet.

If an alien got hold of the record on Wednesday and managed to rustle up a gramophone player to listen to it, a message sent to Earth via radio waves would take a full 24 hours to be received.

Space enthusiasts are also invited to participate in a global event “by creating a wave of golden light.” It sounds rather pointless, but enthusiasts are asked to flash the three-letter call sign for NASA's Voyager mission, VGR, into the night sky - Morse Code style - using their phone flashlights. There’s a website you can open to flash your screen appropriately.

#10450. Anthropic’s IPO filing reveals a strategy to undercut its AI rivals

Welcome to AI Decoded, Fast Company‘s weekly newsletter that breaks down the most important news in the world of AI. I’m Mark Sullivan, a senior writer at Fast Company, covering emerging tech, AI, and tech policy.

Sign up to receive this newsletter every week via email here. And if you have comments on this issue and/or ideas for future ones, drop me a line at sullivan@fastcompany.com, and follow me on X @thesullivan.

‘Compute multipliers’ and ‘Anthropic Direct’ may be the IPO’s secret sauce

As frontier models from Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google converge in capabilities, the companies selling them may end up competing for enterprise business less on model quality and more on the cost of the computing power needed to run them. In its IPO filing and investor roadshow video, Anthropic, which debuted on the Nasdaq on Thursday, suggested it may be preparing for that future with something called “compute multipliers” and a compute-sourcing model it calls Anthropic Direct.

In its S-1, filed publicly in October, Anthropic defines compute multipliers as “algorithmic and methodological” improvements in the way it trains and operates models, effectively increasing the computing power it can get from a given amount of capacity. And these multipliers are “stackable.” In its roadshow video, Anthropic says it measures “total effective compute,” which is its physical computing capacity multiplied by the multipliers it has discovered or expects to discover in the future. Its example: If a model takes 100 units of compute to train, a 4x multiplier lets Anthropic train the same model with 25 units, or use all 100 units to train a model that would previously have required 400.

The company also says the multipliers “stack,” with each new discovery building on previous ones, and that it expects Claude will eventually be able to discover multipliers on its own.

According to the filing, the gains apply to models used to serve customers as well as to model training. Anthropic says its researchers “have delivered meaningful compute multipliers for inference,” reducing the computing power needed to deliver a given level of model performance. The company says this “allows us to provide greater value for customers.”

Anthropic has already been cutting prices. It says price reductions tied to new model versions, along with contractual discounts, reduced revenue growth by about $600 million between the second and third quarters of 2026. It says Opus 5.5, launched in September, delivered “a lower cost per task” than earlier models. If Anthropic can get more usable compute out of each chip than its rivals can, it may be able to undercut other AI labs on price. It may also be able to undercut cloud providers that sell AI services built on their own models.

If compute multipliers let Anthropic do more with its physical computing power, Anthropic Direct could give the company greater control over where that power comes from. Right now, Anthropic buys almost all its computing power from cloud providers, including competitors like SpaceX, Amazon Web Services, Microsoft, and CoreWeave. The company says it has already committed to buying roughly $900.9 billion in compute from these providers over the coming years and decades. Those expenses also include short-term cloud compute purchases, mainly to cover peak usage periods, which come at a premium.

The S-1 says Anthropic is reducing its reliance on expensive cloud providers by developing its own data centers and leasing the chips that go inside them. Its first Anthropic Direct facility came online this year. The company says a “significant portion” of its planned compute spending will go toward building more Anthropic Direct capacity. Based on an analysis of contract values in the S-1 filing, PitchBook estimates that Direct data centers will supply about 1% of Anthropic’s available compute capacity this year, 48% in 2030, and 60% in 2035.

The S-1 says Anthropic’s total compute pool, including third-party cloud compute and Direct, will be used for its own research and model development, as well as customer workloads. Bringing more compute in-house could dramatically reduce the overhead costs of developing and serving Claude models, apps, and agents for enterprise and consumer customers. That, in turn, could allow Anthropic to lower per-token prices for enterprises and subscription rates for consumers.

But Anthropic Direct may end up being something more. The filing doesn’t specifically say Direct compute could be rented to enterprise customers. Still, it’s a possibility; Anthropic could be building an AI-native cloud where enterprises could store their proprietary data and run Anthropic’s models in the same secure environment, potentially at a lower cost than building the same setup within an Amazon, Google, or Microsoft cloud.

That would give the Anthropic Direct brand name a very different meaning. Instead of accessing Claude models through a cloud provider they already use, customers would come directly to Anthropic. That could turn computing from a major overhead expense into a service Anthropic controls and rents to others for profit—a significant change to the company’s business model.

Some big obstacles stand in the way of such an ambition. Google, Amazon, and Microsoft are currently Anthropic’s largest compute suppliers, as well as the main distribution channels through which enterprises buy Claude. The S-1 notes that the three companies are at once Anthropic’s “investors, customers, distribution partners, and competitors.” If Anthropic challenged their cloud businesses directly, it would almost certainly strain those relationships. On the other hand, as more Direct data centers come online, Anthropic’s dependence on those cloud partners could decrease.

If the current rough parity among frontier models continues, the company that can deliver intelligence at the lowest overall cost per task—not per token—may have the edge. Anthropic’s filing suggests it is working toward that position on two fronts: getting more out of each chip and controlling more of the infrastructure those chips run on. Have retail investors factored that strategy into the price they’re willing to pay for Anthropic stock? The answer may emerge only after the stock has traded for a week or so.

California sues OpenAI over rogue AI agents

The California attorney general, Rob Bonta, sued OpenAI on Monday, alleging the company developed and tested advanced AI models without adequate safeguards. The suit centers on a July incident in which OpenAI agents escaped a testing environment and breached the systems of AI platform Hugging Face.

The complaint says OpenAI told the state it has lost control of its autonomous agents more than 80 times during testing. Bonta called the Hugging Face attack the “predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI” that puts growth ahead of safety. The state alleges violations of California’s unfair competition law and seeks an injunction, civil penalties, and disgorgement of profits. An OpenAI spokesperson said the suit “appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab.”

Jensen Huang says he’d be ‘honored’ to return as Nvidia CEO. Its board says nah

Nvidia’s board rejected the idea of reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO just hours after Huang said on Twitter that he’d be “honored” to return. On the company’s earnings call Tuesday afternoon, Harvey Jones, the board chair, said the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” The board had unanimously accepted Huang’s resignation. He has drawn support from Elon Musk, President Trump, and a petition with about 180,000 signatures, but the board is continuing its search for a permanent successor. Colette Kress, the CFO, is serving as interim CEO.

Huang broke his silence Tuesday, less than a week after resigning amid a personal conduct scandal and an investigation. In a statement on X, he said that if the board decides his return is in the best interest of shareholders, employees, the company, and America, “I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.” Huang acknowledged making “serious mistakes in my personal life,” and said, “I own my mistakes completely.” He also said he is “committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation.” 

Demis Hassabis’s Isomorphic Labs raises $5 billion

Isomorphic Labs, the AI drug-discovery company founded and led by Demis Hassabis and spun out of Google DeepMind, announced a $5 billion Series C round of funding on Tuesday. Greenoaks and Sequoia Capital led the round, with participation from Andreessen Horowitz and other new investors and continued significant investment from Alphabet. Several existing backers—Thrive Capital, MGX, GV, CapitalG, Temasek, and the U.K. Sovereign AI Fund—also invested.

Isomorphic will use the money to scale IsoDDE, its drug-design engine built on AlphaFold-related technology, and to push drug candidates toward clinical trials. In a post on X, Hassabis said the company continues “to make rapid progress reimagining drug design from first principles with AI” to cut the time and cost of finding new medicines. No valuation was disclosed, but Bloomberg had reported the company was in talks to base the round on a valuation of about $50 billion.

#10449. 10 Best AI App Builders I've Used in 2026 (and What Each One Gets Wrong)

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

AI App Builders are exploding in popularity, and for good reason. It’s never been easier to build real, functional apps and internal tools using app builders. To test them all, I built the same app on 10 of the most popular AI app builders and tested each across usability, cost, correctness, and ease of use. Most of them can turn a paragraph of description into something that looks like software within a single session. The differences show up around the tenth prompt, when you learn what each edit costs and who has to fix the code once something breaks. I took every price from the vendor's own pricing page on October 29, 2026.

TLDR: Of the best AI app builders I've used, Softr is the one I'd hand to a team that needs auth, data, user groups or integrations. The other nine I tested include code generators such as Lovable and Bolt and visual platforms such as Bubble and Glide, and each one carries a cost or upkeep trade-off worth seeing before you commit.

I looked at the same seven things in every tool, from the first prompt onward:

Softr gets used a lot by operations and business teams as their AI app builder for secure client portals, internal tools and other business apps, none of which require code. Write a short brief in your own words, and the AI Co-Builder turns it into a database plus the core app that sits on it: tables, pages and layouts, the data connections behind them, plus user groups and permissions, so real users can sign in from day one. Workflows come as the next step, either by prompting the Co-Builder again or by adding them in the visual editor.

The Free plan is $0 for unlimited apps, with room for 5 app users, 3 builders, 5,000 records and 5 AI credits each month. Basic runs $19 per month, Pro $99 and Business $329, all on annual billing. Enterprise pricing is custom and includes SSO and SCIM for organizations managing access at scale. The full plan table sits on Softr's pricing page.

Lovable builds full-stack web apps through conversation, writing React code while it takes care of hosting, SSL and the backend. It's designed to move a founder or product team from a prompt to a shareable prototype, and the preview updates as the agent works.

Base44 calls itself a no-code AI platform: you explain the app, and it generates the structure, design and logic while running the backend itself. Authentication, a database and analytics come on every plan, Free included.

Base44 is free for 25 message credits a month. Starter costs $16 per month and Builder $40 per month, both on annual billing, with Pro at $80 and Elite at $160.

Bolt is a coding agent that writes full-stack projects in the browser and runs them on Bolt Cloud, which supplies hosting, databases and integrations. It suits people who want to watch the code take shape and edit it themselves.

Bolt Free is $0 with 1M tokens a month and Bolt branding. Pro costs $25 per month with 10M tokens, and Teams runs $30 a month for each member on monthly billing.

Replit pairs its Agent with a cloud workspace, so a description turns into a running app whose sign-in, database, hosting and monitoring come wired up. The homepage pitches it to people who don't code, though the result underneath is a code project.

Core costs $20 per month ($18 with annual billing) and Pro costs $100 per month ($90 with annual billing). Enterprise is custom and adds SSO, SCIM and audit logs.

Glide starts internal business apps from whatever you hand it, whether a spreadsheet, a written prompt or a PDF, and its newer platform, GlideOS, reads a sheet's structure and relationships to draft screens and workflows. Its apps grew up on phones, and that heritage still shapes the product.

Glide Free is $0 with limited credits. Basic costs $25 per month, Plus $50 per month and Pro $125 per month; annual billing isn't offered yet, according to Glide.

Bubble Free gives you 50K workload units and 500 AI credits each month. Web plans run $32 per month for Starter, $119 for Growth and $349 for Team, all on annual billing.

Retool is an internal tools engine aimed at engineering teams. You describe or assemble an app that connects straight to production databases, APIs and LLMs, with auth and access controls in place at deployment.

v0 generates full-stack Next.js web apps from a prompt and deploys them to Vercel, with Design Mode for visual tweaks and GitHub sync for the code. It's designed around a developer's workflow.

v0's Free plan gives new users $5 of one-time credits and caps messages at 7 per day. Plus runs $30 a month per user, and Business $100 a month per user.

Figma Make turns prompts and Figma design context into code-backed prototypes and web apps you can publish at a URL. It can also scaffold a Payload backend with a database, APIs, auth and an admin panel, or connect to Supabase for sign-in and stored data.

Figma's Starter plan is free with up to 500 AI credits a month. Figma lists a Professional Full seat at $16 per month with 3,000 AI credits, and Organization Full seats cost $55 per month on annual billing.

Collins Dictionary named "vibe coding" its Word of the Year for 2025, and the phrase now covers any workflow where you describe software in plain language and an AI produces it. AI app builders package that workflow with hosting, data and sign-in, so a non-developer can get from idea to something clickable without installing anything.

The questions buyers ask have turned plainer since then: what each edit costs, who keeps the app running, and whether a client can sign in and see their own records alone. A generated front end makes a good demo, and a team using it every day needs permissions and a predictable bill for the next hundred edits.

Softr is now my default when recommending AI app builders. It handles teams, auth, and real company data better than any other product. The AI Co-Builder drafts tables, pages and user groups, workflows follow as the next step, and the app keeps running on maintained platform components with no codebase to patch. App-user pricing and an editor that works without AI credits keep later changes from turning into a running meter.

Three situations call for a different tool. Glide makes a better mobile-first choice when the app spends its days on phones in the field. Bubble gives more front-end design freedom when a project calls for bespoke layouts, interactive animation or heavy brand styling. If your engineers want version control and audit logs and can handle a technical setup, Retool covers that need.

Agents are moving inside the apps these tools produce. Gartner expects task-specific AI agents inside 40% of enterprise applications by the close of 2026, against under 5% in 2025, so a 2027 app builder will need to host agents that respect the same permissions as human users.

Building is also leaving the builder's own window. The Model Context Protocol now sits under the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation and reports more than 97 million SDK downloads a month, with client support in ChatGPT and Claude, among others. Softr's changelog dates its official Claude and ChatGPT connector to October 6, 2026, and I expect more teams to start an app from the chat assistant they already use.

The caution comes from Gartner too: it predicts organizations will scrap upward of 40% of agentic AI projects before 2028, citing escalating costs, unclear business value and inadequate risk controls. Going into 2027, I'd judge any builder on whether it keeps agent costs and access rules visible to the team running the app.

Neville Naidoo is a technology journalist covering AI, startups, and the digital economy, with a focus on how emerging technologies are constantly evolving and shaping our everyday life.

#10448. Have you ever been told that there was something about you that was ‘too much’?

Inflection points spark reflection. And currently, I’m at two inflection points: approaching 10 years of being in business and the end of another calendar year. One of the things I am recalling is that as a woman, some of my characteristics that I once thought of as deficits have conspired to be my greatest assets. Unbeknownst to me, they are actually the factors that contribute to my success.

For example, I am indecisive. I constantly weigh the pros and cons of a situation. I blame that in part on being a Libra — but that trait is also why I loved studying cultural anthropology and gravitate towards multidisciplinary work. In my job history I was sometimes told that I had to “pick a lane.. And it’s been brought to my attention multiple times, especially in corporate environments, that decisiveness is a winning attribute. But as I have evolved, my indecisiveness is the very quality that helps me consider multiple perspectives and identify alternative future scenarios of a situation. Ironically, my indecisiveness helps me navigate ambiguous terrain. 

How wonderful that years later that ability to straddle lanes and work in multidisciplinary environments has become my asset as I’ve built a company to help people toggle between wonder and rigor. 

What about others?

I was curious to learn from other women if an inherent quality that they were told was “too much” turned out to be a creative asset in their work. Bear with me — I know that such a question could be posed to men too. But in my experience, it’s women who tend to contort themselves in order to fit into the workplace. This phenomenon is called “covering.” According to a 2024 Deloitte report in collaboration with the NYU Meltzer Center, covering is when people feel the need to downplay certain identities in order to fit in at work. The report found that cisgender women are more likely to cover than are cisgender men. So for the purposes of this exploration I am focusing on women.  

Sheila Lirio Marcelo, the founder and CEO of Ohai and founder of Care.com shared a time when two mentors took her to lunch to tell her that she was “too intense.. She was able to take the feedback and reflected in the following way:

“They were right. I cared enormously about the work, but I hadn’t yet learned to separate my intensity about the outcome from how I showed up with people. That conversation changed how I lead. I developed a mantra: Be intense about outcomes, but chill with people.”

First, what maturity in Sheila’s ability to take that feedback! Second, what a great reframe on her part. She never disavowed herself of her innate intensity. Instead she converted that intensity into a creative asset. As Sheila put it, that intensity was “the drive to question what others accept, imagine a different answer, and keep pushing until we build it- while giving people the space and trust to get there.”

Daisy Auger Dominguez, Chief People Officer at Digital Asset shared a similar story:

“I’ve been told that I bring too much passion and joy to work, as though enthusiasm somehow diminishes seriousness or credibility. 

“Early in my career, I sometimes felt pressure to temper both to be taken seriously. But I’ve learned that joy and rigor aren’t mutually exclusive. My passion fuels my curiosity and creativity, and joy creates the conditions for others to imagine, contribute, and take risks alongside me. Some of my most meaningful work has come from bringing people together around possibilities they couldn’t yet see. What was once considered “too much” became how I bring others along.”

The lesson

There’s a lesson here for all of us who manage women. I call it inside-out leadership: the ability to be more transparent, humble and curious about the inner lives of those we lead and of ourselves. Consider the following questions:

  • Are there qualities in some of the women on your team that are innate personality traits that could be assets, as in the case of Daisy Auger Dominguez?
  • How might you draw that out in them?
  • Is it worth having a constructive conversation, as in the case of Sheila Lirio, so that you help the woman reframe it as an asset?
  • Are you, as a manager, covering? Could that be to your and your team’s detriment?
  • Or, are you transparent about your unique qualities and encourage your teammates to heighten theirs for the betterment of the work? 

These questions are a starting point to ensure that women thrive, that work flourishes, and that in a time when AI can do basic tasks, we add texture to our work by leaning into what makes us uniquely human.
