#10445. Chase confirms cyberattack that may have exposed customer data. Here’s what we know

Chase Bank isn’t doing much to reassure customers.

The bank said Thursday that third-party vendors were recently targeted in a cyberattack that resulted in a breach of some customer information. But there is “no connection” between this cyberattack and the outage earlier this week that saw customers unable to log in to their accounts, the financial giant posted on X.

“Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses,” Chase said in the post, without specifying when the breach occurred.

JPMorgan Chase, parent company of the bank, was one of several financial institutions to experience outages on Monday that left many customers unable to log in to their accounts for several hours. A string of high-profile outages over the past week has upended work and air travel, while keeping Americans locked out of various websites. Even a highly classified network for internal communications at the National Security Agency experienced an outage.

“Another day, another data breach” shouldn’t surprise most Americans at this point. But paranoia has been proliferating online about a more coordinated takedown of our tech infrastructure—and even though Chase said the cyberattack and outage are unrelated, some people aren’t buying what the largest U.S. bank is saying.

The New York-based company previously blamed the disruptions Monday on a “software bug” that’s since been resolved and said there was no evidence of a cyberattack or a systemic issue. 

So to announce a cyberattack a few days later has only raised more questions. A spokesperson for JPMorgan Chase declined to provide further comment to Fast Company beyond the statement posted on X.

Cybernews reported on Thursday that the ransomware gang n0n dumped stolen data belonging to roughly 16,000 JPMorgan Chase customers and over 100 employees on the dark web after a 48-hour ransom deadline passed. According to the outlet, the leaked information appears tied to Chase’s premium Reserve credit card program that’s marketed to affluent Americans.

The most popular comment on a subreddit discussing that news report came from a Redditor who posted: “We are being lied to by the government.”

That sort of refrain has become increasingly common as people grow more paranoid that something nefarious is happening.

RUBIO TRIES TO REASSURE

Conspiracy theories have flourished online in the wake of these outages, and that’s led some Americans to panic-buy items at Costco, as Bloomberg reported. Meanwhile, a petition on Change.org to “demand full transparency” about these recent tech disruptions has yet to garner much support.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio has seemingly taken on the task in the Trump administration of trying to calm the nerves of Americans. Speaking on Tuesday during a trip to Asia with President Donald Trump, Rubio said the government has “no evidence” that the outages are linked or that they’re the result of cyberattacks, as Politico reported. 

“We fully acknowledge that this is unsettling to see these reports, day after day, of some technical failures,” Rubio told reporters on Tuesday. “We have no evidence, no indications of any kind that these incidents are related to each other or that any of them have anything to do with a malign actor, with a cybercriminal.”

#10444. Trump, Xi, and Putin hold rare summit but deliver no breakthroughs on nuclear risks

For U.S. President Donald Trump, the meeting with the leaders of two other nuclear powers—China’s Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin—was supposed to be a diplomatic triumph: It would serve as proof that Trump could negotiate with two of America’s toughest rivals.

Before the trio met Thursday in a villa in the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen, the U.S. president sought to flatter both Xi and Putin as his friends. They were to discuss the wars in Ukraine and Iran and how to reduce the dangers posed by nuclear arsenals.

But after roughly 70 minutes behind closed doors, they agreed to a far narrower agenda. They would like to reform the United Nations, refine more fossil fuels, and curb the reach of the International Criminal Court.

What was billed as a historic trilateral meeting in the end looked like a fleeting photo op. Trump quickly left the villa and boarded Air Force One without saying a word to reporters about his time with Xi and Putin. Still, he hailed the visit as “highly consequential” on social media as he made his way back to Washington and announced he would hold a press conference on Friday at the White House.

The agreements stemming from the trilateral meeting were modest, but the rhetoric that came at the start of it was not.

“We are really making history,” Trump said. “The United States, Russia, and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth and also to lessen the risk of those weapons being used.”

Xi earlier said the meeting would focus on “promoting world peace.” Putin, for his part, said the countries “hold joint responsibility for maintaining international peace.”

After the meeting, Xi called it positive, constructive, and fruitful, while Putin described the trilateral talks as open and candid, calling the format “useful and substantive.”

“It is a serious collaborative work,” he said in response to a question about whether the image of the meeting itself mattered more than the substance.

The last nuclear arms pact between Russia and the United States, known as New START, expired in February, and Trump has said he wants “a new, improved, and modernized” deal that includes China. But China has less motivation to accept limits given that its arsenal of more than 600 warheads is far smaller than the more than 5,000 warheads believed to be in each of the U.S. and Russian stockpiles.

Daryl Kimball, executive director of the Arms Control Association, said the meeting could at best start a process that would eventually lead to a sustained set of talks for reducing nuclear arsenals.

“We need more than diplomatic theater and photo opportunities between Xi, Putin, and Trump,” Kimball said. “And one meeting will not likely produce dramatic breakthroughs.”

The leaders also talked about Iran and trade

The U.S. president earlier had a separate one-on-one with Xi, their third substantial meeting this year.

Trump said they had a shared interest in having oil flow through the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for oil shipments from the Middle East that was repeatedly shut because of attacks in the Iran war. Trump suggested he would push Xi to buy more agricultural products from America.

Xi said that relations between the U.S. and China have been “generally stable and improved” during Trump’s presidency. The official Chinese news agency Xinhua reported that Xi discussed Taiwan with Trump and said the two countries needed to improve communication on economic and trade issues.

Trump also added to his calendar a separate sit-down with Putin, marking the first time the leaders have met for talks since their discussions in Alaska last year that failed to broker a deal on Russia’s war in Ukraine.

“Wonderful things can come out of this—or at least start,” Trump said, calling Putin “my friend.”

Trump has frequently boasted of his rapport with Putin, as relations between the U.S. and Ukraine appear to have cratered recently. Trump rejected new Russia sanctions, while Kyiv was undermined by disruptions in satellite support for its drones during the war.

After their trilateral meeting, the three leaders took aim at the International Criminal Court for overstepping its jurisdiction, saying government officials should enjoy immunity from its prosecutions. Putin is wanted by the court, and Trump’s administration has imposed sanctions on ICC officials and the institution itself as part of a campaign to dismantle the tribunal over investigations into the United States and its allies, including Israel.

Trump boasts about his relationships, but the ties between Xi and Putin are stronger

The U.S. president’s ambitions going into the meeting recalled an era of great power politics when wealthier countries felt entitled to decide the fate of seemingly lesser nations. Trump was negotiating with China and Russia without the involvement of Ukraine—or allies like Germany, France, the United Kingdom, Japan, and South Korea that also have stakes in the outcome of any talks.

Trump has long believed his ability to create personal connections gives him a diplomatic edge. Xi made a symbolic gesture of friendship Wednesday by taking the unusual step of greeting Air Force One on the tarmac, and the two leaders turned their handshake into a one-armed hug.

But for all the compliments the U.S. president has showered on the two autocrats, he did not always appear to have the same deep relationship based on common interests that Xi and Putin share.

On Wednesday at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, Xi greeted Putin by calling him “my old friend.” The Russian leader responded by declaring Xi to be his “dear friend.” China has helped economically support Russia after its 2022 invasion of Ukraine, providing Putin with a financial lifeline after the U.S. and its allies imposed new sanctions.

By contrast, when Xi went to the White House for a state visit in September, he was far more restrained with Trump, saying they had built a “personal rapport and stayed in touch.” Trump and Xi have one more meeting planned this year, at the G20 summit in Florida in December.

There were also signs of friction Thursday in the U.S.-China relationship despite Trump’s praise of Xi.

Chinese officials blocked a Bloomberg reporter from the trilateral meeting after she asked a question at the earlier Trump-Xi session. And Chinese television showed a video of Trump appearing drowsy, while the White House posted a clip of Trump helping Xi up an escalator.

—By Josh Boak, Michelle L. Price, and Eduardo Castillo, Associated Press

Associated Press writers Darlene Superville, Didi Tang, Will Weissert, Huizhong Wu, and Kanis Leung contributed to this report.

#10443. Gemini rolling out 66 new regional voices on Android and iOS, including 10+ UK dialects

Following a preview at Google I/O, Google is rolling out 66 new regional voices to the Gemini app on both Android and iOS today. The expansion introduces tailored voice options across U.S. English, U.K. English, Indian English, Hindi, Brazilian Portuguese, Indonesian, and Korean.

For users in the UK, the update brings over 10 distinct English voice options covering a wide range of regional cadences. The lineup includes Geordie, Scouse, Brummie, Scottish, Welsh, Northern Irish, Modern RP, and Multicultural London English (MLE).

This might help reduce the issues that sometimes still occur when English accents, in particular, morph into a hybrid of Australian or even American that has been going on for a while with Gemini Live. We have not yet been able to test to confirm this has been resolved with the update. As someone with a regional English accent, this extra representation with Gemini voices is quite welcome.

According to Google, these voices are tuned for natural pronunciation, pitch, and everyday local rhythm rather than exaggerated stereotypes. Because the focus is on cadence over slang, Gemini will sound like a local without filling its text responses with forced street slang. Once selected, your chosen voice carries across the entire app, applying to both Gemini Live conversations and standard text-to-speech playback when tapping the “Listen” icon on chat responses.

You can preview and select the new options today by tapping the three-dot menu inside Gemini Live, or by heading into the Gemini app settings and selecting “Gemini’s voice.” It’s worth noting that the voices aren’t explicitly labeled by city or region in the app menu, and Gemini isn’t programmed to self-identify which accent it is using if you ask it directly.

Instead, Google notes that locally rooted prompts about food, culture, or sport, such as asking for the best pub in Sheffield for a Sunday roast – my suggestion is not a pub; it’s Turnip & Thyme on Eccleshall Road, FWIW. Or another suggestion from big G is where to find proper ingredients for a traditional Scouse stew; the company says these will naturally bring out the warmth and rhythm of the new dialects.

I’d suggest trying to ask where to get the best pattie and chips in Hull or where to get the best pint in Leeds (it’s Whitelocks).

#10440. Measles is back, and it’s a dire warning against shrinking the U.S. government

Sometimes, you really don’t know what you’ve got ’til it’s gone. Take, for instance, the United States’ measles elimination status. Formally rescinded this week, after a 26-year run, the Pan American Health Organization’s new determination is about to make a lot of people realize what a quiet miracle it was to never have to think about measles.

Unfortunately, this genre of realization stands to become a lot more common. The official return of measles is just the starkest domestic example yet of the consequences that come with being led by an administration pot-committed to shrinking the federal government.

The U.S. spent the last century building institutions that provided federal education programs, environmental regulations, consumer protections, and other services benefiting the public. Although these institutions didn’t always work perfectly, they generally either improved U.S. citizens’ lives or shielded them from harm that local governments weren’t equipped to manage on their own. And for at least the 45 years since Ronald Reagan famously declared government was not the solution to America’s problem, but rather the problem itself, tearing down these institutions has been a holy-grail goal for some conservatives.

The most ardent proponents of that goal saw in Trump 2 a glimmering opportunity to dismantle the administrative state, as outlined extensively in the Project 2025 agenda. With the architect of Project 2025, Russell Vought, installed as White House budget director, the last two years have seen the steady evaporation or reorientation of institutions like the Department of Education, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), and of course, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), whose current incarnation helped usher in the measles resurgence.

That result may be a preview of what happens when we lose mechanisms that solve certain problems so thoroughly that people seem to forget they were ever problems in the first place. It’s proof that weakening public protections doesn’t remove the need for those protections; it just makes us much less ready to combat everything they were protecting us from.

How we got measles again

Hours before news broke about America’s measles elimination status, current head of HHS Robert Kennedy Jr. used social media to respond to a different breaking news story. He posted on X an AI-generated image of himself mimicking the photo Amazon MGM used to promote Robert Pattinson as the new James Bond. In the image, a tuxedo-clad Kennedy is holding an enormous carrot instead of 007’s gun, and the caption reads: “Food. Real food.”

It would be hard to find a more apt representation of Kennedy’s tenure as the agency’s leader—a ridiculous, self-aggrandizing folly that depicts Kennedy as laser-focused on improving the quality of Americans’ food while actively ignoring the measles catastrophe he helped create.

Vaccination rates had already been declining since the pandemic, when hesitancy and outright opposition spread virally through so-called wellness influencers and other bad actors. Instead of addressing this trend as the dire threat it was, Trump put in charge of HHS someone who has promoted anti-vaccine positions for decades. Within months, Kennedy was undermining the conventional wisdom around measles vaccinations in settings as public as the Dr. Phil TV show.

Even more damaging: Kennedy kicked off his time at HHS by cutting $11 billion in state and local public-health grants. Those cuts forced health departments across the country to reduce staff, scale back critical services and, yes, either trim down or close various vaccination programs. Suddenly, the wastewater inspections, outbreak response teams, and buses traveling to areas riven by vaccine hesitancy were cut off at the knees.

Amid Kennedy’s efforts to change the childhood vaccination schedule and dispute the number of measles cases and deaths, the U.S. has reported 5,412 confirmed cases through November 13—more than double the 2,289 cases recorded in all of 2025. State health departments have also reported 10 measles-related deaths so far this year, up from three last year. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, cases have now surfaced in 46 states as well as Washington, D.C.

This is exactly the sort of result HHS’s supposedly bloated budget existed to prevent.

Shrinkage

The same governing philosophy that helped set U.S. measles prevention back to the 1950s has also led to downsizing in several other institutions over the past two years—with even more devastating consequences in some cases.

Shortly after Trump’s second inauguration last year, his White House functionally destroyed the United States Agency for International Development (USAID), the primary department coordinating foreign development and humanitarian assistance around the globe. Before January 2025, USAID had approximately 13,600 employees; by April, only 241 remained. Annual U.S. foreign aid disbursements fell by $26 billion throughout the year, and the White House canceled roughly $80.5 billion in USAID and State Department foreign aid awards.

Although Secretary of State Marco Rubio issued a waiver for lifesaving humanitarian assistance programs, he added a laundry list of politically charged exemptions. These included programs involving abortions, family planning, “gender or DEI ideology programs,” and transgender surgeries. Because HIV/AIDS prevention didn’t fall under that waiver, and thanks to severe cuts to the George W. Bush-created President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR), 1,700 HIV treatment sites have since closed. One-year estimates of the global death toll from the loss of USAID stand at around 781,000, and long-term projections are in the range of 14 million. 

Beyond the staggering human toll, there’s bound to be a less obvious domestic cost from the justified erosion of goodwill and diplomacy wrought by this administration’s callous actions.

Stateside, the Trump White House has also taken an axe to the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), arguing that disaster relief should be shifted to individual states. Never mind the obvious risk of exhausting state budgets, creating uneven recovery patterns, and losing large-scale coordination for major crises—the prospect of weaning disaster-stricken Americans off the government teat was simply too attractive!

Through staffing reductions that reduced FEMA’s workforce by 17% last year, terminated grants that left billions in funding up in the air, and the addition of administrative hurdles, FEMA is now much weaker than it was before inauguration. That weakness has thankfully only reared its head in relatively mild ways thus far. No domestic disaster in Trump 2 has yet been substantially exacerbated by FEMA Lite. A lot of disaster fund requests in that time have been delayed or denied, however, and a disproportionate amount of them have been in Democrat-led states.

Meanwhile, slashing roughly 28% of the Treasury Department’s workforce has degraded taxpayer services; hollowing out the CFPB has cost Americans $15 billion in overdraft and credit card late fees alone; and gutting the Office for Civil Rights within the Department of Education has slowed or recklessly dismissed thousands of discrimination cases. 

Little by little, the value of having high-functioning federal infrastructure is starting to become harder for anyone not in deep denial to dismiss or ignore.

The toothpaste is out of the tube

Perhaps the worst part about Trump and his enablers diving whole-hog into dismantling the administrative state is that it won’t be rebuilt any time soon, if ever. It’s a whole lot easier to swing a wrecking ball, after all, than it is to mount an ambitious construction project (unless it’s a ballroom-size monument to the president’s ego).

When experienced staff leave specialized jobs, they often leave a crucial knowledge gap in their wake. When working relationships with outside agencies and other countries are severed, it takes a lot of time and effort to forge new ones—especially if those previous partners now consider your team unreliable. And when research and data collection projects come to a stop because of lost grant money, they seldom start back up again.

Many of the problems Americans now face because of our weakened institutions, and the ones we may face in the near future, cannot be resolved with the stroke of a pen from an incoming majority-Democrat government. For instance, Kennedy could be impeached on January 4 and billions in public-health grants restored the day after, and the U.S. would still be far away from where we stood in January 2025. An epidemiology professor at Johns Hopkins University recently estimated it will take at least five years to reclaim measles elimination status in the U.S.

Getting rid of measles required decades of unflashy work involving vaccination campaigns and other public-health initiatives. Getting rid of our elimination status took less than two years.

If we ever want to get it back, not only will we have to play the Uno Reverse Card on much of what’s happened during Trump 2, but we’ll also have to collectively let go of the myth that strong federal institutions are somehow the biggest problem in America, rather than a source of solutions.

#10438. Elon Musk claims he’s ‘not MAGA’ in the wake of the blue wave

Since President Donald Trump’s reelection in 2024, Elon Musk has been one of his biggest allies in Silicon Valley. The Tesla CEO has served as both Trump’s employee and his friend: He spearheaded the Trump administration’s Department of Government Efficiency, aka DOGE, and wasn’t shy to tell the press that he came to “love” Trump over the course of their work together.

But in an interview at this week’s annual DealBook Summit, Musk suddenly sang a different tune.

“I’m not MAGA,” Musk said. “I’m not sure what MAGA means, but if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don’t have that.”

Musk may claim not to know the full extent of what “MAGA” means, but in the lead-up to the 2024 presidential election, he was happy to embrace the term. Wearing an infamous black MAGA hat to one of Trump’s rallies at Madison Square Garden, Musk told the crowd that he’s “not just MAGA,” but “dark gothic MAGA.”

Now, though, after the country’s historic shift to the left in this month’s midterm elections, Musk is positioning himself as bipartisan. “I think there are positives and negatives in both parties,” he said.

Musk’s historic midterm spending

Musk’s recent actions make it hard to believe he doesn’t consider himself bound to the Republican Party. Ahead of the midterms, the world’s richest man became the largest individual political donor in U.S. history, giving $446 million to conservative PACs including his own America PAC, which he founded in 2024 to support Trump’s presidential campaign.

But according to Musk, that record-breaking spending wasn’t in direct support of Republicans, but in support of a politically balanced Congress. His goal—“which failed, by the way,” Musk joked—was for Republicans to hold 51 seats in the Senate in 2029. 

“I think we want to have at least one of either the presidency, the House, or the Senate be of the other party,” Musk said.

But the blue tsunami proves that Musk’s investment didn’t pay off. He says he feels “pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it.”

He added: “Probably, if I could rewind the clock, I would have spent less money.”

Musk’s donations included hefty sums in his home base of Texas, where two Republican candidates he backed, Gov. Greg Abbott and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, lost to Democrats Gina Hinojosa and James Talarico, respectively.

But Musk is looking on the bright side, saying he believes that Hinojosa “is going to be quite moderate” as governor.

“Based on everything I’ve heard about her, I think things will be fine in Texas with Gina as governor,” he said. “I don’t think she’s a far-left governor.”

A blue wave in tech?

Musk isn’t the only tech titan to downplay their GOP affiliations in the wake of the midterms. Last week, Palantir CEO Alex Karp claimed the software company’s products are “essentially progressive” despite its contracts with the Trump administration, including creating surveillance technology for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

“I’ve been a Democrat my whole life. I grew up in a far-left environment,” Karp said. “I know more about being a progressive than almost anybody on the planet, and I absolutely believe Palantir—all of our products are essentially progressive.”

Like Musk, Carp said his support of Republicans has been in service of political moderation, not a right-wing takeover.

“My giving is equal Democrat, Republican,” Karp said. “I can tell you, without going into things I’m not gonna disclose, I’m very balanced, and everyone in the political arena knows it. And I’ll tell you what—I’m also not the village idiot.”

#10435. An Army explosion could send toxic lead dust across multiple states. Here’s what residents need to know

The U.S. Army is planning to blow up roughly 5 tons of bomb-making materials in Iowa on Friday, a volatile event expected to send a plume of toxic lead dust into the air as far as 90 miles away. The chemicals are unstable enough that moving them poses a high risk of explosion, a fact that makes a planned detonation the comparatively safe option.

The unusual event may sound like a side quest straight out of Grand Theft Auto VI, but it holds potentially serious health consequences for people in the area. The detonation is set to take place at noon Central time at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, a small town in the southeast corner of the state. 

The Army described the planned explosion’s hazards in an advisory to local residents, noting that the long-stored barrels of unstable lead azide are expected to create elevated levels of airborne lead when detonated. The advisory states that lead levels are expected to remain below the threshold “at which EPA would require protective actions be taken,” but goes on to describe many measures that residents should take to protect themselves during the event.

“The detonation will result in an air plume with some lead-containing particles which will disperse in the air and deposit on the ground,” it continues. “Residents in Middletown will hear a loud noise; feel vibrations from two consecutive, rapid detonations; and see a plume of dust which is expected to linger for no more than one hour after the detonation, depending on wind speed.”

The explosion is expected to be large enough that locals close to Middletown City Park and Butterfly Park could experience “localized window damage.” Residents have been asked to leave their houses for six hours on the day of the detonation, as both locations are less than a quarter of a mile from the detonation zone.

2 lead exposure pathways pose serious dangers

The Army is also cautioning people who live or work nearby to avoid the area, stay indoors, keep windows closed, and set their heating and cooling units to recirculate air within their homes in order to minimize potential exposure. Schools in communities including Danville and Mediapolis will close Friday to protect students from lead exposure—both airborne dust and settled dust.

“Deposition of lead-containing dust may occur after the detonation on surfaces within certain areas affected by the detonation plume,” the Army’s warning states, encouraging residents to wet-clean surfaces exposed to the chemical dust after the explosion takes place. The advisory, which also includes a map predicting the path of the toxic dust, warns that children, pregnant women, and older adults in particular should avoid contact with lead particles. 

Only about 400 people live in the Iowa town where the blast will take place, but toxic dust is expected to drift into the air and deposit itself 30 miles north in more populated neighboring communities like Morning Sun, Mediapolis, and Wapello. Airborne lead dust could cause problems to people who inhale it as far away as Cedar Rapids, which is 90 miles from the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant. 

Even Illinois, the state next door, is on high alert for the explosion. “There is no safe level of lead in the body, and when inhaled or swallowed, it can pose serious health risks,” Dr. Sameer Vohra, director of the Illinois Department of Public Health, said in a health advisory. “Illinois residents who may be affected by the detonation can stay safe by staying indoors and keeping windows closed for 24 to 48 hours.”

#10434. Young people may be holding back gender equality at work

About two decades ago, a substantial body of academic research started to provide evidence for what many had long suspected: Young people were leading the way toward a more gender-equal world.

European Social Survey data from 2004 and 2010 found that younger adults were considerably less likely than their older counterparts to endorse traditional gender roles. In 2009, Pew Research found that Americans under the age of 30 were considerably more liberal in their attitudes toward women’s roles than older generations. And in 2015, a study published in Psychology of Women Quarterly found that millennials held more egalitarian attitudes toward women’s work and family roles than baby boomers had at the same age.

The direction of travel seemed clear: Each new generation was broadly more supportive of gender equality than the last.

Over the last few years, though, there’s been a disconcerting shift. In several recent surveys, young men—and in some cases young women—have expressed more traditional attitudes toward gender roles, and greater skepticism about efforts to advance women’s equality, than men old enough to be their fathers or grandfathers.

And there’s evidence that this generational divide extends to attitudes toward leadership, too. This month, the Reykjavík Index for Leadership—an annual study conducted by global research firm Verian and the Reykjavík Global Foundation, an Iceland-based nonprofit—found that younger adults are considerably less likely than their older counterparts to believe women and men are equally suited to lead. 

“The assumptions around sociodemographics and values and attitudes that we were able to make until the 2020s no longer hold in the same way,” says Michelle Harrison, global president at Verian Group and cofounder of the index. “We understand we are in a new geopolitical and technological paradigm.”

The findings raise troubling questions for businesses that have spent decades working to advance gender equality: What happens when the next generation of leaders appears less convinced of its importance than the last? And what can organizations do to change people’s minds? 

A growing generational divide

Launched in 2018, the Reykjavík Index measures perceptions of gender-equal leadership across 23 sectors, from politics to technology. Its latest survey questioned more than 11,000 adults across the G7—Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom, and the United States—and four other countries, asking whether men, women, or both are equally suited to lead. A score of 100 represents universal agreement that men and women are equally suited to leadership.

After reaching a peak of 73 in 2019, the G7’s overall index score has steadily declined. This year, it edged up for the first time in seven years, rising one point to 69. But the modest recovery masks a real generational divide. 

Across the G7, 18- to 34-year-olds recorded an index score of just 65, compared with 74 among 55- to 65-year-olds. The gap itself is not new—it has existed since the index was launched in 2018—but it has tripled from three to nine points in that time, and the youngest group’s score has also fallen five points over the same period.

The divide is particularly stark in Britain and France, where younger adults trail their older counterparts by 14 points. And while young men’s attitudes have shown signs of improvement in several countries over the past year, the broader picture remains troubling. Younger adults are still the least likely to view men and women as equally suited to lead.

These findings corroborate other studies. In 2025, a 30-country study by Ipsos and King’s College London found that Gen Z men and women were more divided on questions of feminism, gender roles, and women’s rights than any other generation surveyed. Some 57% of Gen Z men agreed that efforts to promote women’s equality had gone so far that they discriminated against men, compared with 36% of Gen Z women and 44% of boomer men.

The power of the manosphere

Experts offer different explanations for what has caused the generational shift in attitudes. Many, however, mention social media’s ability to shape cultural scripts. 

“Contemporary online communities such as the manosphere are vocally opposed to women behaving in agentic or assertive ways. This includes in the home and in the workplace,” says Rachael Robnett, a professor of psychology and director of the Women’s Research Institute of Nevada at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas. “To the extent that young men are disproportionately engaged in the manosphere relative to other generations, it makes sense that they would show less positive attitudes about women’s leadership ability,” she adds. 

Jess Carbino, a sociologist and author, agrees. “I believe the generational divide may reflect cyclical changes happening in how feminism and gender roles are being signaled in the media, particularly on social media,” she says.  

Another possibility, Carbino suggests, is that we’re witnessing a backlash against changing economic and social norms. The share of women who earn as much as—or significantly more than—their husbands has approximately tripled over the past 50 years, according to Pew Research data. For a brief period earlier this year, there were more women in non-farm payroll jobs in the U.S. than men, according to federal data. 

These changes have challenged long-standing assumptions about men as breadwinners and women as caregivers, and for some men, Carbino suggests, that shift can feel threatening.

“When masculinity feels threatened—by earning less than a partner, for example, or by losing status at work—some men withdraw from domains culturally coded as feminine, like caregiving and housework,” she explains.

Such responses can reinforce the very stereotypes that gender-equality initiatives have sought to dismantle: assumptions about who should lead a company, who should earn the family income, and who should stay home to raise children.

Related to this, Kent Bausman, a professor of sociology at Maryville University of Saint Louis, says that economic pressure and economic insecurity can “breed a sense of zero-sum gain in the competition for jobs and resources.” Young men who are “still socialized as the traditional economic provider interpret women’s expansion in opportunities across various walks of life as a threat to their own economic prospects,” he adds.

A workplace opportunity

For Harrison, the latest findings present employers with both a challenge and an opportunity. While the generational divide threatens to complicate efforts to advance gender equality, workplaces may also be among the most important settings in which attitudes can change.

Unlike the online spaces where young people may encounter rigid ideas about masculinity and femininity, workplaces can expose them to different models of leadership, collaboration, and authority. Seeing women succeed in senior positions and men thrive in roles traditionally associated with women helps to challenge assumptions about who is suited to lead.

Carbino argues that employers can make those examples more visible, creating opportunities for employees to learn from leaders who defy traditional expectations.

“Employers can elevate and highlight women’s leadership,” she says. “They can engage in programs in which women mentor both men and women.”

Ultimately, Carbino remains hopeful that the “pendulum will swing back.” Historically, she notes, periods of backlash against feminism have often been followed by renewed progress.

Robnett, too, cautions against interpreting the findings as evidence that an entire generation has rejected gender equality. Although some young men hold more traditional attitudes than their older counterparts, not all of them do.

“Although we need to continue to push for change in these negative attitudes, it is encouraging that most young men perceive women and men as equally suited to leadership roles,” she says.

Indeed, there are tentative signs of progress: The G7’s overall index score has begun to recover, and young men’s scores have risen in five of the seven countries surveyed.

Whether that recovery lasts remains uncertain, Harrison says. But, she adds, the findings suggest that the next generation’s attitudes toward gender equality are not set in stone—and that the workplaces they enter could help shape what comes next.

#10431. College may cost much less than you think, according to this calculator tool from the University of Pennsylvania

A quick Google search for the yearly cost of attending the University of Pennsylvania returns a flat figure: $99,082.

But that remarkably high number doesn’t tell the full story. Nearly half of Penn students receive financial aid, with 68% of those students having all of their tuition and fees covered by need-based assistance. But prospective students and their families often don’t know whether they’ll fall into that group, instead daunted by the university’s projected $100,000 price tag.

The uncertainty around the cost of college contributes to Gen Z’s declining interest in four-year degree programs. As of 2026, just 37% of college graduates say they believe their degree was worth the cost, while less than half of high school students in the U.S. (44%) say they expect to earn a bachelor’s degree. The latter stat, from a 2022 survey, marked a 20-year low for college expectations.

That’s why Penn has joined a growing cohort of universities offering cost calculators to students, using information like family size and income to project a student’s cost of attendance long before they’re ever admitted.

Calculator culture

To use Penn’s cost calculator, prospective students and their parents input data from their tax forms (or the forms themselves) as well as information like their marital status and the number of college students in their family currently enrolled. The calculator then returns a four-year estimate of the cost for that student to attend Penn, taking into account their projected need-based aid. 

While the calculator takes time to return a result, it also offers a selection of sample families to compare with. Are you closer to Hana, whose family makes $37,000 and has 86% of her tuition covered by Penn, or Nathan, whose family makes $425,000 and is paying the full tuition cost themselves?

Another college offering a cost calculator is Brandeis University, which launched a tool called FAYE (an acronym for “financial aid you can expect”) in May. Brandeis also offers academic merit-based aid, so FAYE takes students’ transcripts into account along with financial and family data.

Other colleges offer less-sophisticated estimates of students’ annual costs, not with calculators, but with graphs. Take Yale’s instant net price estimator, which shows a low, high, and best estimate of cost based on a family’s annual income. More than 60 other schools offer similar tools in collaboration with the College Board.

#10430. Top 6 AI Detector Tools in 2026: Features, Accuracy Claims and When to Trust Them

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

AI writing tools are now part of everyday work for students, marketers, developers and editors, and a parallel category of tools has appeared to answer one question: was this text written by a person or a model? Teachers, publishers, hiring teams and content managers use these detectors to screen submissions, but the technology is probabilistic, its accuracy claims vary, and the cost of a wrong call can be high.

This guide compares six AI detector tools, CudekAI, GPTZero, Copyleaks, Originality.ai, Turnitin and Sapling, on what their own pages state. It then explains how detectors work, summarizes the research on their limits, and ends with a short script you can use to test any detector on your own samples. The tools are listed in no ranking order. Feature details, limits and prices change often, so confirm current information on each vendor’s site before you commit.

• A detector gives a probability, not proof. Every vendor in this list warns that results can be wrong, and several advise against using a score alone.

• Limits differ widely. Character limits, supported languages, models detected and free allowances vary between tools and even between pages of the same tool.

• Bias and short text are known weak spots. Research has found detectors misclassify some non-native English writing, and most vendors say accuracy improves with longer text.

• Vendor accuracy claims are not comparable. Figures come from different datasets, thresholds and models, so test on your own material.

• Use detection as one signal. Combine it with drafts, version history, interviews or other evidence before acting on a result.

CudekAI’s AI detector returns an AI percentage and a human percentage for pasted text, with paragraph, sentence and word-level analysis for mixed documents. According to its page, it also accepts PDF and Word files with per-page scores and downloadable reports, and offers separate code and image detectors. The page lists models it says it detects, including ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Llama, DeepSeek and Grok, and says it supports more than 100 languages.

Strengths: sentence-level highlighting, file uploads with reports, and extra detectors for code and images in the same product.

Limitations and gaps: the page shows different character limits in different places, including 1,000, 5,000 and 15,000, so check the limit that applies to your plan. It says to start free but does not state a free allowance, and it lists detection as costing one credit. A headline accuracy figure of 99 percent appears in its page metadata, while the body refers to independent benchmarking without naming sources, and its FAQ says accuracy may vary for mixed or paraphrased text and that false positives can occur. API access is listed under an enterprise plan.

Fits: writers and teams who want a quick check with sentence-level detail and file reports, and who will verify results rather than rely on a single percentage.

GPTZero gives an overall score and highlights flagged sentences, and adds a Writing Replay feature that records the writing process, including typing patterns and paste events. It also lists a plagiarism checker and integrations with Google Docs, Google Classroom, Canvas, Zapier and a Chrome extension, plus an API.

Strengths: process-based evidence through Writing Replay, strong education integrations and published benchmark figures. On the RAID benchmark, the page reports 95.7 percent of AI text detected and 1 percent of human text wrongly flagged.

Limitations and gaps: it claims full support for five languages (English, German, Portuguese, French and Spanish) and says other languages lack stated accuracy levels. The company’s own page says no detector is 100 percent accurate, that results should not be the final verdict, and that accuracy is higher on longer English text. The free scan box has a 10,000-character limit, and plan prices are not listed on the page.

Fits: educators and editors who want writing-process evidence as well as a score.

Copyleaks describes an AI detector covering more than 30 languages and models including ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek and Llama. Its AI Logic feature explains why text was flagged, and it says it can detect AI-generated code. It offers a browser extension, a Google Docs add-on, learning-management-system integrations and an enterprise API.

Strengths: explanation of flagged text, code detection, broad integrations and published per-language accuracy figures, which range from 93.08 percent for Portuguese to 99.20 percent for English on AI text, according to the page.

Limitations and gaps: the figures are the vendor’s own. It claims a 0.03 percent false-positive rate and cites a 2023 study, so treat the number as a claim to verify on your data. Free scans cover up to 25,000 characters, but paid plan prices sit on a separate pricing page.

Fits: organizations that need multilingual coverage, code detection or integrations.

Originality.ai combines AI detection with a plagiarism checker and a fact and hallucination checker. It lists sentence-level highlights, a mixed AI and human category in its newer detection models, a Chrome extension with a writing replay feature and an AI detection API.

Strengths: several checks in one product, an API with documentation and a clear statement of limits. The page acknowledges false positives, says very short text under a 100-word minimum and AI rewriting tools can affect results, and advises against using the score alone.

Limitations and gaps: it is credit-based, free scans are capped at 100 credits per account and credits expire two years after purchase. Its accuracy claims cite third-party studies and internal benchmarks that you should review yourself.

Fits: publishers, agencies and SEO teams that want detection, plagiarism and fact checks in one workflow.

Turnitin is built for educators and institutions. Its AI writing detection estimates how much of a submission is human-written versus likely AI-generated, including likely AI-paraphrased content, and works inside learning-management systems alongside similarity checking.

Strengths: deep institutional integration and unusually explicit framing of results as probabilities. For documents above its 300-word minimum, the page reports false-positive rates of 0.014 for English language learners and 0.013 for native English writers and concludes there is no statistically significant bias. It also links guidance on handling suspected false positives.

Limitations and gaps: it is aimed at institutions rather than individual freelancers, the page does not give an overall false-positive figure, and it describes detection as just one piece of a broader challenge. Mention of language support is limited, with a linked post about Arabic.

Fits: schools and universities that already use Turnitin and want detection within the same workflow.

Sapling offers an AI content detector with a free check of the first 2,000 characters, and Pro and Enterprise accounts can check up to 100,000 characters. It provides a free API key and documentation, and it publishes unusually candid guidance on limits.

Strengths: transparent caveats and a developer-friendly API. The page says false positives and negatives may occur, that accuracy varies with dataset, text length and threshold, and advises measuring results on your own examples. It also warns that some tools claiming to be undetectable falsely say they passed its detector.

Limitations and gaps: accuracy improves after about 50 words, non-English text is scored by the English model for unsupported languages and is described as less reliable, and prices are not listed on the page. A reported 60 percent drop in false positives comes from internal evaluations that the page does not publish.

Fits: developers and teams that want to integrate detection and test it on their own data.

The table summarizes what each page states. It is not a benchmark, and “not stated” means the page did not say, not that the feature is absent.

• False positives. Human writing can be flagged, especially when it is short, formulaic or highly predictable.

• Bias risk. A research paper titled GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers found that the detectors it tested consistently misclassified non-native English writing as AI-generated, and warned against using such detectors in educational settings. Turnitin’s page reports the opposite for its own tool, which is a reason to test on your population.

• Evasion. Paraphrasing or editing AI text can lower scores. The same research found that simple prompting strategies could both reduce bias and get text past detectors.

• Mixed authorship. A document that is partly AI-assisted can get a low overall score while individual sentences score high, as Sapling’s page points out.

• Moving targets. New models change the text distribution, so a tool trained on older models can lose accuracy.

• Shifting benchmarks. Vendors report different datasets and thresholds, so numbers are not comparable.

OpenAI’s own experience is a useful reminder. Its AI text classifier correctly flagged 26 percent of AI-written text on a challenge set while mislabeling 9 percent of human text, and the page states that the classifier was withdrawn on July 20, 2023 due to its low rate of accuracy. Detection has improved since, but the underlying difficulty has not gone away.

Most detectors are classifiers trained on large collections of human-written and machine-generated text. They look for statistical patterns, such as how predictable the word choices are or how uniform the sentence structure is, and output a probability. Some systems add features such as sentence-level scoring, writing-process data, or checks for hidden provenance signals.

• Statistical signals. Text that a language model finds highly predictable tends to look machine-like, which is why formulaic human writing can be misflagged.

• Trained classifiers. Detectors learn from labeled examples and update as new models appear.

• Writing-process evidence. Tools such as Writing Replay record how a document was typed or pasted, which is stronger evidence than a style score.

• Provenance. Standards such as C2PA Content Credentials aim to record the origin and edits of content when the creating tool supports them, which is different from guessing after the fact.

Because vendor figures are not comparable, the most reliable approach is to measure. Build a small labeled set that reflects your real content, including human writing from different groups of authors, and calculate false-positive and false-negative rates by group. The script below wraps any detector behind a single function. The stub is a placeholder, so replace it with a call to the tool you are evaluating and follow that vendor’s API documentation.

is_ai: bool        # ground truth you control

group: str = "all" # e.g. "native", "non-native", "technical"

def evaluate(detect, samples, threshold=0.5):

"""detect(text) -> probability the text is AI-generated (0..1).

Wrap any vendor API or tool export in this function."""

g = stats.setdefault(s.group, {"fp": 0, "human": 0, "fn": 0, "ai": 0})

g["fn"] += not flagged          # AI text that slipped through

g["fp"] += flagged              # human text wrongly flagged

fpr = g["fp"] / g["human"] if g["human"] else float("nan")

fnr = g["fn"] / g["ai"] if g["ai"] else float("nan")

print(f"{group:12} false positive rate {fpr:.1%}  false negative rate {fnr:.1%}")

return 0.9 if "delve" in text.lower() else 0.2

Sample("Let us delve into the topic.", True, "native"),

Sample("I wrote this note by hand.", False, "native"),

Sample("We delve into methods used here.", False, "non-native"),

Sample("The results were reviewed twice.", True, "non-native"),

With only a handful of samples the numbers mean little, so use a larger, representative set and report results per group, because an acceptable overall rate can hide a high rate for one group.

• Never treat a score as proof. Use it to start a conversation, not end one.

• Gather corroborating evidence. Drafts, version history, writing-process data and discussion with the author carry more weight than a percentage.

• Tell people how detection is used. Publish a policy so authors know what to expect and how to appeal.

• Check for bias. Test on writers like those you evaluate, including non-native speakers.

A tool that estimates how likely a piece of text is to have been generated by an AI model, usually as a percentage, often with sentence-level highlighting.

They can be useful, but accuracy depends on the text, length, language and threshold, and every vendor in this guide states that errors can occur. Test on your own samples.

Yes. False positives are acknowledged by vendors and documented in research, particularly for short or formulaic text and some non-native English writing.

Free tiers are fine for a quick check, but they have limits on length and features, and the result should not be the sole basis for a decision.

Sometimes. Paraphrasing and editing can lower scores, and partly AI-generated documents can produce mixed results.

A plagiarism checker looks for matches with existing sources. An AI detector estimates whether text resembles machine-generated writing, which is a different and less certain task.

AI detectors are useful screening tools, but none is a verdict. The six reviewed here differ in language coverage, limits, integrations, explainability and how candidly their pages describe error, and their accuracy figures come from different tests. Compare them on the factors that matter for your content, measure false positives on your own samples, and combine any score with other evidence before acting on it.

Turns old Game Boy cartridges into a chiptune jukebox.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A new device on Kickstarter claims to make Game Boy cartridges relevant again by playing soundtracks from your favorite classic Nintendo games. The Retro Song Bird is a box-shaped speaker that supports Game Boy and Game Boy Color cartridges, with support for over 1,900 games. Simply inserting a cartridge into the speaker gives you access to all soundtracks and sound effects, which can be controlled using onboard physical controls including next, previous, and volume.

The Retro Song Bird also comes with a 3.5mm stereo line-out and a USB Type-C port in case you want to connect to other audio equipment. According to the developer, it offers accurate, register-level sound emulation and can be used to sample and remix music from your Game Boy cartridges. It exposes all four audio channels (two square, wave, noise) as separate USB audio streams that can be imported into a DAW. This allows you to isolate individual melodies, waveforms, and sound effects from old games to create your own melodies. There’s even support for LSDj for playing saved chiptune tracks, while two Retro Song Bird units can be synced for DJ-style performances using Game Boy cartridges instead of traditional records.

In addition to playing retro video game soundtracks, the Retro Song Bird also supports the Game Boy Camera, allowing you to use it as a webcam offering a glorious 128×112 pixels resolution and 5 frames per second speed. Other features include the ability to back up and restore save files, ROMs, flash writable carts, and export any soundtrack or sound effect as WAV onto your PC. The listing also includes other abilities, including an Alarm Mode, a record of every cartridge you've ever plugged in, an open API for developers, and over-the-air updates.

The Retro Song Bird is currently available to back on Kickstarter, with the standard model starting at $79. The introductory $59 Early Bird offer has already sold out, while the developer is also offering a two-unit bundle for $150. Shipments are expected to begin in April 2027.

The developer notes that only a handful of hand-assembled prototypes currently exist and that the hardware and design still need some refinements. The project also faces potential manufacturing challenges, including component availability, finding suitable manufacturing partners, and producing injection-molded enclosures. Like any other Kickstarter campaign, delivery timelines are subject to change, and backers should be aware that there is no guarantee the finished product will ship as planned.

#10428. How to manage a post-IPO workforce that just became fabulously wealthy

Anthropic’s $1.5 trillion initial public offering instantly turned thousands of its roughly 5,300 employees into multimillionaires.

Like other companies that have undergone massive IPOs, Anthropic is now facing a challenge: how to keep the trains running with a workforce where many employees may no longer need to work. Indeed, studies show that employees at post-IPO companies are more likely to leave their jobs or become less satisfied.

Management experts and executives who have successfully navigated IPOs say there are a few ways companies can make sure that doesn’t happen.

GIVE EMPLOYEES A REASON TO WORK OTHER THAN MONEY

The most important thing is to make sure workers have a sense of purpose that goes beyond making money, something Google cofounders Larry Page and Sergey Brin highlighted explicitly in a letter to prospective shareholders when the company went public in 2004.

“Talented people are attracted to Google because we empower them to change the world,” they wrote. “We are focused on providing an environment where talented, hardworking people are rewarded for their contributions to Google and for making the world a better place.”

Laszlo Bock, who oversaw Google’s human resources operations for a decade following its IPO, echoed that sentiment nearly 10 years later.

“We spend more time working than we do on almost any other activity in our lives,” he wrote. “People want all that time to mean something.”

Of course, it is ideal if that sense of purpose is already in place before a company goes public.

“If a company’s employees are coming to work just to make money, it’s over,” venture capitalist Paul Koontz said in 2004. “There need to be some bigger ambitions, some more fundamental calling that motivates a company.”

GIVE WOULD-BE ENTREPRENEURS FREEDOM TO EXPERIMENT

One of the biggest risks for post-IPO companies is that their most talented and entrepreneurial employees now have the resources to launch their own ventures. In fact, the effect is so powerful that at least one study has identified a causal link between the rate of IPOs in the economy and the rate of new firm creation.

While it may be impossible to prevent these exits altogether, post-IPO companies should ensure that their most talented staff have the freedom and resources to pursue their own ideas.

“There has to be safe space for entrepreneurial employees,” Syracuse University professor Carl Schramm said in 2018. “There has to be some space where people can actually try and push an idea around, scope it out, have a friendly ear someplace in the hierarchy of the company.”

Management should also consider giving top talent their own discretionary research budgets. In the mid-2010s, Adobe launched a program that gave its workers $1,000 to spend however they liked, with no explanation or justification required.

“When you trust people, they’ll live up to your expectations,” Mark Randall, formerly Adobe’s chief strategist and VP of creativity, told Fast Company. “They’ll allocate their resources and figure out how to move ahead.”

DON’T LET WEALTH CREATE A NEW OFFICE HIERARCHY

IPOs can create an awkward social dynamic in which employees’ wealth bears little relationship to their seniority, or even their contributions to the company. This can leave managers supervising employees who have several times their net worth, and newcomers resenting colleagues who got rich doing the same basic job.

Post-IPO companies should acknowledge this dynamic instead of pretending it doesn’t exist. Ahead of Google’s IPO, clinical psychologist Stephen Goldbart recommended that companies organize workshops for employees to discuss how their newfound wealth affects workplace relationships, job expectations, and corporate culture.

“The biggest mistake a company can make is to pretend [an IPO] has no impact,” he said.

Executive compensation consultants Todd Sirras and Austin Vanbastelaer also recommend giving managers more power to reward top performers, including by “increasing responsibilities, expanding strategic opportunities, and promoting visibility and engagement with senior executives.”

PAY ATTENTION TO WELL-BEING AND WORKING CONDITIONS

Employees at startups often put up with grueling hours and difficult work conditions, knowing they may be in line for a big payoff. Once the payoff arrives, however, their tolerance for those things may go away.

And new stressors will emerge, including increased bureaucracy, regulatory burdens, and the pressure to meet quarterly earnings. One study that analyzed 3.7 million Glassdoor reviews found that employee ratings of senior management and work-life balance declined 10% and 6.6%, respectively, following IPOs.

Post-IPO companies must keep their finger on the pulse of their workforce to identify any percolating dissent. For example, in the run-up to Google’s 2004 IPO, Silicon Valley executive coach Laura Hollands-Steck advised companies preparing to go public to survey employees about how to improve working conditions.

Management may also need to take their foot off the gas pedal a little bit. In a study published earlier this year, researchers from the University of Alabama and the University of Iowa examined the management practices and long-term survival of 183 companies that went public in 1996.

They found that companies are more likely to survive if executives strike the right balance between maintaining a sense of urgency and valuing employees.

“Too little sense of urgency can lead to complacency while too much urgency can lead to burnout, lower quality output, and other undesirable consequences,” the authors wrote.

#10424. Secure cloud storage is the cheaper, safer alternative to keeping files physical

Physical storage and memory are only getting more expensive, but that doesn’t mean we need to store any less. The alternative solution is a secure cloud storage platform, and there’s really only one good option.

That extends throughout every platform it’s available on, including Android, iOS, macOS, Windows, and Linux. On just about any platform, users get access to the pCloud Drive app for dedicated storage and backup. On Android and iOS, you have an additional option to automatically back up photos to free up space on your phone. pCloud Photos also acts as a smart photo gallery within the app, and sharing between other pCloud users and friends is made incredibly simple.

No matter where you access your pCloud Drive, all your files are there – safe and secure. You can store all kinds of files in pCloud, including documents, photos, videos, and even documents containing passwords.

Of course, you also get the option to take security a step further with pCloud Encryption. Your most sensitive files can be stored with an added layer of client-side, zero-knowledge encryption. The key is all yours, and no one else’s.

Even if you already have a hefty backup solution like an in-home NAS, pCloud is still a good option because it makes that NAS that much more useful. It has an official NAS backup feature with support for WebDAV, Rsync, SFTP, and SCP. pCloud simply provides another safety net for your existing backup.

Unlike a lot of cloud storage services, pCloud doesn’t charge on a monthly or even yearly basis. Just like buying physical storage, paying once for what you need is enough. But what makes it a better option than going the traditional route – beyond the skyrocketing storage prices – is the features and security that come with it.

This just so happens to be the best time to choose secure cloud storage, too. pCloud’s Black Friday promotion runs from November 13 to November 28. Starting with the base 500GB lifetime storage plan, pCloud’s one-time price comes down to $159 – 43% off. The 2 TB plan is currently down to $379, while the massive 10GB lifetime plan is 61% off at $1,099. pCloud is also offering a bundled 3-in-1 option that includes 3TB of storage, a lifetime pCloud Pass subscription, and pCloud Encryption for $579.

Secure cloud storage has major advantages, and a one-time subscription for terabytes of storage is rare these days.

Another record quarter and strong guidance.

For the first time in its 33-year history, Nvidia on Tuesday reported quarterly financial results without Jensen Huang at its helm or on the call, after its cofounder and longtime chief executive departed five days ago. To no one's surprise, Nvidia continues to set new financial records as demand for its AI accelerators shows no signs of slowing down. The company reported revenue of $115.8 billion for the third quarter of its fiscal 2027, with its latest Vera Rubin platform generating $20 billion. Meanwhile, its supply commitments surged to $390 billion.

"Our momentum is real. NVIDIA is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people," said Colette Kress, interim chief executive and chief financial officer of Nvidia. "Vera Rubin is off to an explosive start, our roadmap is on track, and our ambition has never been greater."

For the third quarter of fiscal 2027, which ended on October 25, 2026, Nvidia posted revenue of $115.844 billion, an increase of 20% sequentially and 103% year-over-year. The company's net income reached $65.287 billion, up 105% from the same quarter last year, while gross margin hit 74.8%. Revenue from the Compute & Networking segment totaled $106 billion, up 20% quarter-over-quarter and 108% year-over-year. Meanwhile, the Graphics segment generated $9.8 billion, a sequential increase of 25% and 62% compared with the same period a year ago.

As expected, Nvidia's results during the quarter were primarily driven by its Data Center business, which generated $107.6 billion in revenue (and accounted for approximately 93% of the company's sales), up 21% sequentially and 110% YoY. Hyperscale customers accounted for $60.1 billion, an increase of 23% QoQ and 71% YoY, while sales to AI Clouds, Industrial & Enterprise customers reached $47.5 billion, up 18% sequentially and 195% compared to the same period last year. Although hyperscalers remain Nvidia's largest customer category, demand from AI cloud providers, industrial companies, and enterprises continues to grow considerably faster on an annual basis. Meanwhile, Edge Computing revenue reached $8.2 billion, up 14% sequentially and 42% year-over-year.

One of the main contributors to Nvidia's growth was its Vera Rubin platform, which generated nearly $20 billion in revenue in its first quarter of production shipments, which Nvidia described as the fastest product ramp in its history. The company also reported strong demand for standalone Vera CPUs and continued sales growth for Blackwell Ultra. According to Nvidia, its hyperscale partners brought Vera Rubin systems into production in approximately one month, which is two times faster than the previous-generation Grace Blackwell platform.

"Vera Rubin is off to an extraordinary start: in its first quarter of production shipments, the Rubin platform generated nearly $20 billion in revenue, making it the fastest product ramp in Nvidia's history," Kress said. "We continue to see very strong demand for Vera and expect total CPU revenue to more than double in FY2028."

To support the expected growth of its AI infrastructure business, Nvidia has substantially increased its long-term procurement obligations. The company's supply and capacity commitments reached $390 billion at the end of Q3 FY2027, compared with $279 billion three months earlier and $119 billion at the end of Q1. Nvidia attributed the latest increase primarily to multiyear memory procurement agreements.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

The company expects to fulfill $69 billion of these commitments during the remainder of FY2027 (which ends in late January), followed by $203 billion in FY2028 and $92 billion in FY2029. Another $26 billion is scheduled for FY2030 and beyond. In other words, Nvidia has already committed to purchasing $390 billion worth of components and manufacturing capacity through the end of FY2030, though given the fact that its purchases in FY2028 are set to exceed $200 billion, expect its procurements in FY2030 to be higher.

The commitments reflect Nvidia's efforts to ensure that its suppliers can manufacture sufficient quantities of advanced processors, memory, substrates, and packaging components. In addition to its existing agreements with partners like TSMC, Micron, Samsung, and SK hynix, Nvidia on Wednesday announced new partnerships with Samsung Electro-Mechanics and Kinsus for substrates, as well as SPIL for advanced packaging. In addition, the company disclosed agreements with Amkor, Ibiden, KYEC, and Unimicron.

During the earnings call, Kress said that demand for Nvidia's products continues to exceed available supply, prompting the company to work with manufacturing partners to expand production capacity. She also indicated that Nvidia could provide suppliers with prepayments or other financial assistance to accelerate capacity expansion.

Although these procurement commitments are gargantuan, Nvidia expects demand for its AI infrastructure to remain strong, which will justify the expenditures. The company raised its revenue growth forecast for FY2028 from approximately 70% to 75% due to stronger demand and additional manufacturing capacity that it expects to secure.

In addition to its supply commitments, Nvidia disclosed $32 billion in agreements with neocloud providers that allow it to earn revenue from hardware sales and participate in cloud rental revenue above a guaranteed minimum. Meanwhile, the company's maximum financial exposure under various guarantees reached $118 billion, including $105 billion in credit support for the PORTS-Pike AI data center campus in Ohio, which will serve OpenAI under 20-year leases.

In total, Nvidia's commitments reached $540 billion as of early Q4 FY2024.

Nvidia currently absorbs higher component and manufacturing costs to honor existing purchase orders and maintain previously agreed prices for its customers. As a result, the company expects its GAAP gross margin to decline from 74.8% in Q3 FY2027 to 71% – 72% in Q4, which it considers the bottom of the current margin cycle.

Going forward, Nvidia plans to introduce revised pricing in FY2028 to help offset higher supply costs and restore profitability, which is when the company expects gross margins to recover to 72% – 73% next fiscal year, although it has not disclosed the magnitude of its planned price adjustments or the products they will affect.

"We thought about in terms of our prices and pieces of that, and a lot of the costs were some of the things that we absorbed in those numbers that we included," Kress said. "What we provided here in Q4 is our bottom. If you recall, that was our bottom as we honored many of the different POs that we had already received from our customers, and we just wanted to make sure that was held solid as we moved to a new pricing, as we moved into the new year."

Perhaps more importantly is that Colette Kress largely sidestepped the question about custom AI accelerators and their potential impact on Nvidia's pricing power. During the conference call, an analyst asked whether Nvidia would accept lower margins to protect its market share against custom AI accelerators developed by hyperscalers. The interim CEO avoided directly addressing whether competition from custom silicon could undermine Nvidia’s competitive position, leaving considerable room for speculation.

For the fourth quarter of fiscal 2027, Nvidia projects revenue of approximately $130 billion ±3%, which would represent an increase of about 12% sequentially. The company expects GAAP gross margin of 71% to 72% and GAAP operating expenses of approximately $11 billion during the quarter. Nvidia’s forecast excludes Data Center compute revenue from China and accounts for an additional week in the quarter. While Nvidia expects its gross margin to decline during the Vera Rubin transition, Kress said that the company anticipates a recovery to 72% – 73% in FY2028.

#10421. New Gemini setting lets you keep chat history, but turn off AI training

Gemini’s existing Keep Activity setting “controls how long your chats are saved and whether they are used to train generative AI models.”

Google is now separating that preference into two new options.

This is huge. One of the major things Siri-AI users on iPhone like to point out is that while their assistant is a less capable portmanteau of Siri and Gemini, their queries are not used for AI training. Gemini on Android, on the other hand, offers the superior AI platform with the caveat that there is no way to opt out of training and still retain your chat history. Until now. Now users of Gemini on Android get the best of both worlds - the best of Google's AI models powering their AI experiences and their chat history siloed from AI training.

The first setting is called “History” and lets you “control how long your history is saved.” If disabled:

“…future chats will be saved for around 2 months and used to respond to you, process your feedback, and protect Google, its users, and the public, with help from human reviewers.”

The duration is currently 24 hours for chat context, and 72 hours to help protect Google, users, and the public.

The second setting allows you to “separately control whether your chat content, including text and attachments, is used to train generative AI models.”

With this change, you will be able to keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training.

If Keep Activity is currently off, the two “new settings will both be off.” These changes are rolling out over the “coming weeks,” and Google is notifying users via email.
